title: A Human-Centered Approach to Interpretable Machine Learning in Clinical Decision Support Systems
journal: 2025 2nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence for Innovations in Healthcare Industries (ICAIIHI)
authors: V. Nimbalkar and L. Chawla and M. M. Adnan and A. Bhansali and M. Gupta and R. Kalra
abstract: Interpretable machine learning (ML) paired with clinical decision support systems (CDSS) is revolutionizing healthcare in the context of enhancing transparency, personalization, and trust. This survey of 25 recent articles demonstrates that explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is essential to enhance clinician adoption and patient outcomes in different clinical settings, such as oncology, emergency medicine, and mental health. Scholars note that to make AI human-centric, promote cooperation between clinicians and algorithms, and provide the transparency of data, researchers need to design AI in a more human-centric manner, which will help to align the use of ML tools with ethical, fair, and realistic principles. Although these have been made, there are still difficulties in the field, including the need to balance model accuracy and interpretability, deal with biases, and incorporate them into current clinical practice. New approaches are being designed, such as the use of electronic health records, engaging end-users in the development of designs, and the use of new approaches of explanations, such as data-centric and proximity-informed explanations.
keywords: Interpretable machine learning;clinical decision support systems;explainable AI;healthcare innovation;human-AI collaboration;ethical AI

title: Exploring the Advancements of AI Enabled Clinical Decision Support Systems for Patient Triage in Healthcare
journal: 2024 IEEE International Conference on E-health Networking, Application & Services (HealthCom)
authors: J. M. R. Mejia and D. B. Rawat
abstract: As the demand for medical services grows, the need for an efficient care process becomes increasingly urgent. Recent events have highlighted that the demad for services exceeds the available supply. In response, the focus of heaht information technology has shifted toward advanced clinical decision support systems (CDSS) to addess the critical challenges facing the medical industry. However, many healthcare organiztions lack robust clinical systems and tools. This research presents a comprehensive study of current industry applications, its related works, and provides insights into optimizing current state of the art machine learning (ML) CDSS with newer technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence-based knowledge graphs. This paper offers an overview of CDSS, details the patient treatment process and triage methods, explores the capabilities of knowledge graphs in healthcare, and underscores the need to incorporate machine learning into these processes to increase intelligence, robustness, and personalization.
keywords: E-triage;Health Record;Generative AI;Knowledge Graph Databases;E-Health;Remote Triage;Healthcare applications;Patient treatment process;Medical Internet of Things;Healthcare

title: Interpretable Machine Learning-Based Triage For Decision Support in Emergency Care
journal: 2023 7th International Conference on Trends in Electronics and Informatics (ICOEI)
authors: H. Mutegeki and A. Nahabwe and J. Nakatumba-Nabende and G. Marvin
abstract: In medicine, triage is a process that rations health services towards patients who are most in need of immediate care. Traditionally, a nurse will carry out an evaluation to ascertain a patient's condition and assign an Emergency Severity Index(ESI) to represent the urgency level needed to attend to them, which is time-consuming and subject to human error and bias. Mistriage could potentially lead to delayed medical attendance and ultimately to death if the condition is not managed, while no triage could overwhelm the finite hospital resources and medical personnel in trying to attend to the huge patient volumes. Existing research in the domain largely focuses on the prediction of patient disposition(whether or not one will be admitted). This work proposes using Explainable AI to generate insights that can support human-in-the-loop Machine Learning triage of patients at the emergency department level. This research utilized Machine learning classification algorithms like the Decision Trees classifier, Random forest classifier, Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting classifier, XGBoost classifier, and ELM Classifier to predict the Emergency Severity Index of a patient based on their medical data. Upon hyperparameter tuning, the models are evaluated and the Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting classifier topped them all as the best-performing model with an average Area Under the Curve(AUC) score of 91 % over the 5 classes and an F1 score of 70%. Explainable AI(XAI) techniques like Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations(LIME) and Shapley Additive Explanations(SHAP) were used to create more transparent and trustworthy algorithms for Intelligent Healthcare.
keywords: Machine Learning(ML);Triage;Emergency Care;Explainable Artificial Intelligence(XAI);Intelligent Healthcare

title: Predicting Post-stroke Hospital Discharge Disposition Using Interpretable Machine Learning Approaches
journal: 2019 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (Big Data)
authors: J. Cho and A. Alharin and Z. Hu and N. Fell and M. Sartipi
abstract: Stroke is the fifth leading cause of death for Americans. Due to critical consequences and cost, an efficient stroke system of care (i.e., acute treatment, post-stroke acute rehabilitation) is necessary. Early determination of hospital discharge disposition is important for stroke management, and can make an immense impact in optimizing acute treatment and planning post-acute rehabilitation with desired outcomes. With the rise of sophisticated machine learning models, many researchers have gained momentum in using such models in their studies. However, due to the lack of explanations that models provide, the integrity of the prediction result is often challenged. Our goal is to predict post-stroke hospital discharge disposition using machine learning models to increase the prediction capability while providing explanations for the results using an interpretation method, such as Local Interpretable Model-agnoistic Explanations (LIME). Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of LIME in providing interpretability to machine learning models and suggests further exploration in performance improvement.
keywords: machine learning;model interpretation;lime;neural network;black-box

title: Evidence-Based Reasoning in Medical Assessment: Collaborating with Physicians in Practicing Argument Development and Evidence Marshalling
authors: Z. An and J. Huang and F. Garner
abstract: People without professional medical knowledge often opt for expensive yet swift emergency room services when they fall ill, placing significant pressure on nurse triage systems. Although Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are widely used in healthcare, they raise concerns about accuracy, bias, fairness, lack of explainability, ethical and legal challenges, and the risk of over-reliance and de-skilling. These issues remain unresolved by researchers. In this paper, we present research conducted in collaboration with physicians, using the scientific method for hypothesis generation, evidence collection, and hypotheses analysis to develop well-reasoned arguments and marshal evidence effectively. By integrating evidence-based reasoning with healthcare expertise, our approach mimics the nurse triage process in emergency departments (ED), offering guidance ranging from life-saving interventions to less urgent care recommendations. This clear, structured analysis-detailing the argument logic, evidence used, and its application-supports the training of less experienced ED nurses, enhancing their critical thinking skills and encouraging rational use of AI tools rather than indiscriminate reliance.
keywords: evidence-based reasoning;medical assessment;nurse triage;healthcare education

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Early Detection of Critical Outcomes in the Emergency Department
journal: 2025 IEEE 38th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS)
authors: W. A. Sulaiman and A. Panayides and E. Schiza and E. Kyriacou and A. Kakas and C. S. Pattichis
abstract: Emergency departments (EDs) require effective approaches for quickly identifying patients at risk of critical outcomes (inpatient mortality or ICU admission within 12 hours). This study developed interpretable machine learning models using Gradient Boosting (GB) and Logistic Regression (LR) with 13 initial triage variables from the MIMIC-IV-ED database. GB performed slightly better than LR (Accuracy: 78.21% vs. 77.27%, AUROC: 0.887 vs. 0.863, AUPRC: 0.445 vs. 0.370). The Te2Rules method was used to extract 43 clinically interpretable rules from the GB model, with a overall fidelity of 98.90%. The use of the Rule Coverage Index (RCI) to categorize rules into high, medium, and low levels futher enhanced clinical utility. This study aims to strike a balance between predictive accuracy and interpretability, facilitating clinicians in early detection of critically ill presenting to the ED.
keywords: Emergency department;Machine learning;Explainable AI;Healthcare analytics;Clinical decision support;Risk stratification

title: AI-Based Clinical Decision Support System for Mitochondrial Assessment in IVF
journal: 2026 World Conference on Computational Science and Technology (WcCST)
authors: A. V and L. S. A and M. K. B. N
abstract: About one in six people worldwide are affected by infertility, fostering a deepened reliance on assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs) like in vitro fertilization (IVF). However, the standard IVF decision-making process often does not include a structured assessment of mitochondrial risks that affect oocyte quality, treatment planning, and qualification for procedures like mitochondrial replacement therapy (MRT). The described system is an AI-driven clinical decision support system (CDSS) that encompasses patient assessment, oocyte mitochondrial health assessment, donor screening and recommendation, and explainable AI. The system performs machine-learning-based triage to select patients who may benefit from a targeted mitochondrial evaluation and builds support for donor compatibility decisions, utilizing both rule-based and data-driven approaches. Explainability has been ingrained through SHAP-based feature attributions to enable clinician trust and auditability. While the full mitochondrial imaging analysis module (CNN-based oocyte morphology assessment) remains future work since data were not available, the actualized modules build an operational decision support pipeline. Results from synthetic datasets show strong calibration, discriminative ability, and interpretable outputs that are amenable to further clinical validation.

title: Consistency of XAI Models against Medical Expertise: An Assessment Protocol
journal: 2024 IEEE 12th International Conference on Healthcare Informatics (ICHI)
authors: E. Arnaud and M. Elbattah and A. Pitteman and G. Dequen and D. A. Ghazali and P. A. Moreno-Sánchez
abstract: Despite the significant advances made by Artificial Intelligence (AI) models in enhancing medical diagnostics and prognostics, their opacity poses a hurdle to widespread clinical adoption. In this regard, Explainable AI (XAI) aims to demystify these complex models, such as neural networks, by revealing the reasoning behind predictions. However, a notable gap exists in enabling non-experts to verify these explanations, necessitating human-in-the-loop evaluation. This paper introduces a systematic protocol, including a novel “consistency” metric, to evaluate the SHAP-based explanations of XAI, comparing them against the clinical knowledge of expert clinicians. We demonstrate how this metric could facilitate both global and feature-specific analyses, operating at the level of individual instances, and thus enhancing AI transparency. It is conceived that the implications of this work may extend beyond the medical context, offering a standardized methodology that could potentially improve the interpretability and acceptance of AI systems in diverse domains.
keywords: Explainable AI;Interpretability;Human in the Loop;Trustworthy AI

title: Explainable AI and Augmented Reality in Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE) Imaging
journal: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and eXtended and Virtual Reality (AIxVR)
authors: R. Harari and A. Al-Taweel and T. Ahram and H. Shokoohi
abstract: This study explores how mocked explainable AI (xAI) decision support system and Augmented Reality (AR) impact clinicians' trust and performance in Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE) imaging. A cohort of 24 Emergency Medicine clinicians assessed three xAI modalities alongside an AR interface. The study found that detailed xAI explanations gained the highest trust and decision accuracy. AR-based decision support was also viewed as innovative, but potentially distracting. Further studies with larger sample sizes in real clinical settings are required to validate these findings.
keywords: Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE);Explainable AI (xAI);Augmented Reality (AR);Clinician Trust

title: Emergency Department Triage Hospitalization Prediction Based on Machine Learning and Rule Extraction
journal: 2023 IEEE EMBS Special Topic Conference on Data Science and Engineering in Healthcare, Medicine and Biology
authors: W. A. Sulaiman and A. Nicolaou and N. Prentza and C. Stylianides and A. Panayides and I. Constantinou and Z. Antoniou and A. Kakas and E. Kyriacou and L. Palazis and T. Kyprianouv and C. S. Pattichis
abstract: The objective of this work was to investigate the usefulness of explainable AI (XAI) functionality in the Emergency Department (ED) triage hospitalization prediction modelling based on machine learning and rule extraction. Prediction modelling was carried out using the MIMIC-IV-ED dataset that contains over 400,000 ED visits for predicting hospitalisation Yes vs No (discharged). The Gradient Boosting (GB) prediction modelling gave the best performance achieving an accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of 83%, 82% and 84% respectively. These results are comparable with previous studies published in the literature. Subsequently, interpretable rules were extracted with a high precision threshold, demonstrating the rules’ overall accuracy in replicating the model’s behaviour. Further work is needed to validate the rules extracted with the ED medical experts as well as to benchmark the findings with other models and studies.Clinical Relevance: The use of explainable AI (XAI) in predicting hospitalization outcomes in the Emergency Department (ED) using machine learning and rule extraction, has the potential to improve clinical decision-making.

title: Early and Accurate Diagnosis of Ectopic Pregnancy: A SHAP-Based Explainable Machine Learning Approach
authors: G. Kocun and I. Yelmen and M. Zontul and F. Yildirim
abstract: Ectopic pregnancy (EP) is a significant cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, particularly in the first trimester. It occurs when a fertilized ovum implants outside the uterine cavity, with the fallopian tubes being the most common location. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical to prevent complications such as tubal rupture and hemorrhage. Traditional diagnostic methods rely on transvaginal ultrasound (TVUSG) and serial  $\beta $ -hCG measurements, but these approaches can sometimes yield inconclusive results. Recent progress in artificial intelligence has demonstrated potential for improving the precision of ectopic pregnancy detection. This study examines the use of artificial intelligence-based classification models to predict pregnancy outcomes using routinely available clinical data. The dataset comprises 310 patient records collected from real-world clinical practice. Several classification approaches were evaluated, with particular emphasis on tree-based ensemble models. Experimental results indicate that the LightGBM DART model outperformed the other evaluated classifiers, achieving the highest overall performance with an accuracy of 0.9161, a macro-AUC of 0.9409, and a balanced accuracy of 0.9080, followed by CatBoost and Histogram-based Gradient Boosting models. To enhance model transparency and clinical interpretability, Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were applied to identify the most influential features contributing to model predictions. These findings suggest that explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-based predictive models may support early and accurate diagnosis during the early follow-up period (Day 0–12), assist clinicians in timely decision-making, and potentially improve patient management, rather than serving as a standalone tool for initial Day-0 triage.
keywords: Clinical decision support;ectopic pregnancy;explainable artificial intelligence;LightGBM DART;machine learning;maternal health;medical diagnosis;predictive modeling;SHAP

title: AI-Powered E-Triage Systems: Enhancing Healthcare Efficiency Through Intelligent Clinical Decision Support
journal: 2026 International Conference on AI Innovations and Industry (ICAIII)
authors: M. Elsersy and A. Abdelwahab
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered e-triage systems are transforming patient intake and clinical decision-making by automating workflows and improving diagnostic precision. These systems address critical challenges in emergency and outpatient settings, where rapid assessment and prioritization are crucial for delivering optimal care. This paper introduces an integrated architecture comprising four core components: a Data Ingestion Module that consolidates patient information from electronic health records (EHRs), wearable devices, and intake forms; an AI Triage Engine employing machine learning algorithms to evaluate patient urgency and predict risk; a Documentation Generator utilizing natural language processing (NLP) for automated admission reporting; and a Prescription Assistant that recommends evidence-based treatments aligned with clinical guidelines. Real-world deployments in hospitals across the UAE and GCC have demonstrated substantial operational improvements, including a 45 % reduction in documentation time and an 82 % increase in patient prioritization accuracy. These advancements not only enhance patient outcomes through early detection of critical conditions but also alleviate clinician workload, reducing burnout and cognitive strain. Key performance indicators (KPIs) such as diagnostic accuracy, patient throughput, and prescription error rates validate the system's effectiveness and scalability. Despite these benefits, challenges remain in ensuring data privacy compliance, mitigating algorithmic bias, and achieving seamless integration with existing EHR platforms. Future directions include incorporating real-time analytics, expanding wearable device interoperability, enabling multilingual support, and adopting human-in-the-loop models to maintain ethical and clinical robustness. By addressing these barriers, AI-powered e-triage systems can become a cornerstone of modern healthcare, delivering adaptive, efficient, and patient-centric care at scale.
keywords: AI in Healthcare;E-Triage Systems;Clinical Decision Support;Machine Learning;Healthcare Automation

title: An Automated Approach for Timely Diagnosis and Prognosis of Coronavirus Disease
journal: 2021 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
authors: A. R. Ali and M. Budka
abstract: Since the outbreak of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19), most of the impacted patients have been diagnosed with high fever, dry cough, and soar throat leading to severe pneumonia. Hence, to date, the diagnosis of COVID-19 from lung imaging is proved to be a major evidence for early diagnosis of the disease. Although nucleic acid detection using real-time reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR) remains a gold standard for the detection of COVID-19, the proposed approach focuses on the automated diagnosis and prognosis of the disease from a non-contrast chest computed tomography (CT) scan for timely diagnosis and triage of the patient. The prognosis covers the quantification and assessment of the disease to help hospitals with the management and planning of crucial resources, such as medical staff, ventilators and intensive care units (ICUs) capacity. The approach utilises deep learning techniques for automated quantification of severity of COVID-19 disease via measuring the area of multiple rounded ground-glass opacities (GGO) and consolidations in the periphery (CP) of the lungs and accumulating them to form a severity score. The severity of the disease can be correlated with the medicines prescribed during the triage to assess the effectiveness of the treatment. The proposed approach shows promising results where the classification model achieved 93% accuracy on hold-out data.
keywords: assessment of treatment;computed tomography;explainable AI;diagnostic imaging;quantification of disease;radiography

title: Triage Level Prediction Using Machine Learning with Tree-Based Gradient Boosting Algorithms
journal: 2025 IEEE CHILEAN Conference on Electrical, Electronics Engineering, Information and Communication Technologies (CHILECON)
authors: J. Moya-Carvajal and F. Tirado and X. A. López-Cortés and A. M. C. Silva
abstract: Triage in emergency departments (EDs) is fundamental in prioritizing patient care and optimizing the allocation of limited healthcare resources. However, conventional triage systems remain susceptible to inconsistencies such as undertriage and overtriage, particularly in high-demand clinical environments. This study presents a machine learning-based approach for predicting triage levels using structured data from the emergency unit of a high-complexity regional hospital in Chile. The dataset was filtered to include only adult and dental consultation records, excluding pediatric and obstetric-gynecological cases due to their different clinical characteristics. Patients were categorized into five triage levels (C1 to C5), revealing a strong class imbalance, with C2 and C3 comprising nearly 90% of all records. The study implemented three tree-based gradient boosting algorithms, XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM, in conjunction with Bayesian hyperparameter optimization and SVMSMOTE to mitigate class imbalance. Data preprocessing involved Random Forest-based imputation, standardization of numerical features, and one-hot encoding of categorical variables. The results indicate that XGBoost outperformed CatBoost and LightGBM in terms of overall accuracy (0.73) and weighted F1-score (0.72), particularly in the most frequent categories (C2 and C3). CatBoost, while exhibiting slightly lower global accuracy, demonstrated greater sensitivity in the minority class C1. However, all three models showed limitations in predicting the C5 category. The main contribution of this work is to demonstrate the feasibility and limitations of multiclass (C1–C5) triage prediction using gradient boosting models with Bayesian optimization and SHAP interpretability under extreme class imbalance.
keywords: Triage of patients;Emergency departments;Clinical decision support system;Machine Learning

title: Early Prediction of In-Hospital Mortality in Emergency Departments Using Ensemble Machine Learning
journal: 2026 6th International Conference on Innovative Research in Applied Science, Engineering and Technology (IRASET)
authors: C. B. Jdira and Y. Yaddaden and M. -D. Rioux and S. Ouellet
abstract: Emergency departments operate under high patient volume and clinical uncertainty, where early identification of patients at risk of in-hospital mortality remains a major clinical challenge. Traditional systems rely on clinician judgment and rule-based scoring, which can be subjective and slow for highacuity patients. We propose an explainable machine learning framework for early prediction of in-hospital mortality using only information available at arrival, thereby aligning prediction with real-world early assessment constraints and avoiding reliance on retrospectively available hospital data. The approach is evaluated on the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care and its emergency department subset, combining structured demographics, physiological data, and unstructured chief complaints. Ensemble models achieved strong predictive performance while remaining interpretable via SHapley Additive exPlanations, highlighting age, initial vital signs, prior emergency visits, and arrival mode as key risk factors. These results demonstrate the potential of explainable artificial intelligence to support early risk assessment and improve the identification of emergency department patients at high risk of in-hospital mortality.
keywords: Emergency department;in-hospital mortality prediction;ensemble learning;explainable artificial intelligence;electronic health records;SHAP

title: Using Data Mining to Predict Hospital Admissions From the Emergency Department
authors: B. Graham and R. Bond and M. Quinn and M. Mulvenna
abstract: Crowding within emergency departments (EDs) can have significant negative consequences for patients. EDs therefore need to explore the use of innovative methods to improve patient flow and prevent overcrowding. One potential method is the use of data mining using machine learning techniques to predict ED admissions. This paper uses routinely collected administrative data (120 600 records) from two major acute hospitals in Northern Ireland to compare contrasting machine learning algorithms in predicting the risk of admission from the ED. We use three algorithms to build the predictive models: 1) logistic regression; 2) decision trees; and 3) gradient boosted machines (GBM). The GBM performed better (accuracy = 80.31%, AUC-ROC = 0.859) than the decision tree (accuracy = 80.06%, AUC-ROC = 0.824) and the logistic regression model (accuracy = 79.94%, AUC-ROC = 0.849). Drawing on logistic regression, we identify several factors related to hospital admissions, including hospital site, age, arrival mode, triage category, care group, previous admission in the past month, and previous admission in the past year. This paper highlights the potential utility of three common machine learning algorithms in predicting patient admissions. Practical implementation of the models developed in this paper in decision support tools would provide a snapshot of predicted admissions from the ED at a given time, allowing for advance resource planning and the avoidance bottlenecks in patient flow, as well as comparison of predicted and actual admission rates. When interpretability is a key consideration, EDs should consider adopting logistic regression models, although GBM’s will be useful where accuracy is paramount.
keywords: Data mining;emergency department;hospitals;machine learning;predictive models

title: Emergency Department Triage Classification: A Comparative Study with Explainable AI for Small-Data Environments
journal: 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Systems, and Emerging Technologies (ICAISET)
authors: A. Saad and T. Houda and S. Houda
abstract: Emergency Departments (ED) overcrowding causes delayed treatment, high mortality, and nurse burnout. Manual triage suffers from inter-rater variability and cognitive load. This paper evaluates an automated triage framework using the Korean Triage and Acuity Scale (KTAS) to risk-stratify ED patients (Emergency vs. Non-Emergency). A total of 1,267 encounters were analyzed (24 structured features plus chief complaint text) to compare 18 models across traditional ML, deep learning, and NLP paradigms. We enforced strict leakage prevention by performing all preprocessing after a stratified train-test split. Tuned Random Forest achieved the top recall of 88.44% (95% CI [0.8333, 0.9324]), prioritizing patient safety, while SHAP analysis confirmed clinically valid predictors like injury and pain severity. Most importantly, our results demonstrate that high-performance, safety-critical triage models can be derived from modest datasets (n ≈ 1, 200) without relying on the massive repositories (n > 100, 000) often cited. This suggests that bespoke, high-recall AI tools are viable for smaller clinics, enabling them to deploy "catered" models that reflect specific local demographics. Our findings illustrate the potential of interpretable ML-augmented triage as a decision-support tool.
keywords: Deep learning;emergency department;explainable AI;machine learning;natural language processing;triage classification

title: Assessment of Hematological Predictors via Explainable Artificial Intelligence in the Prediction of Acute Myocardial Infarction
authors: R. Yilmaz and F. H. Yagin and A. Raza and C. Colak and T. C. Akinci
abstract: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is the main cause of death in developed and developing countries. AMI is a serious medical problem that necessitates hospitalization and sometimes results in death. Patients hospitalized in the emergency department (ED) should therefore receive an immediate diagnosis and treatment. Many studies have been conducted on the prognosis of AMI with hemogram parameters. However, no study has investigated potential hemogram parameters for the diagnosis of AMI using an interpretable artificial intelligence-based clinical approach. The purpose of this research is to implement the principles of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in the analysis of hematological predictors for AMI. In this retrospective analysis, 477 (48.6%) patients with AMI and 504 (51.4%) healthy individuals were enrolled and assessed in predicting AMI. Of the patients with AMI, 182 (38%) had an ST-segment elevation MI (STEMI), and 295 (62%) had a non-ST-segment elevation MI (NSTEMI). Demographic and hematological information of the patients was analyzed to determine AMI. The XAI approach combined with machine learning approaches (Extreme Gradient Boosting, XGB; Adaptive Boosting, AB; Light Gradient Boosting Machine, LGBM) was applied for the estimation of AMI and distinguishing subgroups of AMI (STEMI and NSTEMI). The SHAP approach was used to explain the predictions intuitively. After selecting the 10 most important hematological parameters for AMI, the LGBM model achieved 83% and 74% accuracy for prediction of AMI, and distinguishing subgroups of AMI (STEMI and NSTEMI), respectively. SHAP results showed that neutrophil (NEU), white blood cell (WBC), platelet width of distribution (PDW), and basophil (BA) were the most important for AMI prediction. Mean corpuscular volume (MCV), BA, monocytes (MO), and lymphocytes (LY) were the most important hematological parameters that distinguish STEMI from NSTEMI. The proposed model serves as a valuable tool for physicians, facilitating the diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of patients with AMI and distinguishing subgroups of AMI (STEMI and NSTEMI). Analyzing readily accessible hemogram parameters empowers medical professionals to make informed decisions and provide enhanced care to a wide range of individuals.
keywords: Acute myocardial infarction;NSTEMI;clinical classification;explainable artificial intelligence;SHAP;hematological parameters

title: Tuberculosis Detection Based on Multiple Model Ensemble in Chest X-ray Image
authors: A. -C. Tsai and Z. -G. Zhou and Y. -Y. Ou and I. J. -F. Wang
abstract: Tuberculosis is a legal infectious lung disease, a chronic infectious disease caused by tuberculosis. The diagnosis of the confirmed person is usually judged by chest X-ray images, and the sputum smear is used to detect the presence of tuberculosis in the sputum. Screening high-risk individuals can effectively prevent the spread of tuberculosis; however, chest X-ray image interpretation and sputum testing take a long time. When infectious tuberculosis patients are found, tuberculosis has already spread. We propose a tuberculosis diagnostic triage system and a tuberculosis detection system based on preprocessing of lung image segmentation. In the tuberculosis diagnosis and triage system, AI interpretation is performed immediately after the patient's chest X-ray is taken, and abnormal tuberculosis cases are immediately listed. Lung field cropping through U-Net for classification in the form of a multiple ensemble system, including the use of EfficientNet-BO, Densenet121, and Xception. After marking abnormal lung images, we use a tuberculosis detection system to find patients with tuberculosis and use GRAD-Cam to display the image areas that are of most interest to the model, similar to a heat map, allowing us to know the model Predicting focus areas for tuberculosis. We used specificity, sensitivity, accuracy, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) to evaluate the classification model performance.
keywords: convolutional neural network (CNN);chest Xray(CXR);tuberculosis classification;diagnostic triage;lung field cropping;gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM)

title: Development and Validation of an Explainable Deep Learning Model to Predict Adverse Event During Hospital Admission in Patients with Sepsis
journal: 2022 IEEE/ACIS 23rd International Conference on Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, Networking and Parallel/Distributed Computing (SNPD)
authors: I. -M. Chiu and Y. -P. Chuang and C. -Y. Cheng and C. -H. R. Lin
abstract: Sepsis is among the most common conditions requiring emergency hospitalization. The early and accurate identification of sepsis patients with a high risk of in-hospital adverse events can aid physicians in making optimal clinical decisions. This study aimed to develop an explainable neural network model to predict adverse events during hospital admission in patients with suspected sepsis. Patient data were collected from a single medical center in Taiwan for the period of 2018–2020. The adverse events considered during hospital admission were cardiac arrest, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, and transfer to intensive care unit during admission. This study included 9398 patients in the analysis, with 6794 and 2603 patients in the development and validation sets, respectively. The proposed model could predict adverse events with an area under the receiver operating curve of 0.88 and 0.85 in the development and validation sets, respectively. Of the 2603 patients in the test set, 523 (20.1%) were classified as having adverse events during hospital admission. Of these patients, 104 eventually experienced adverse events. Thus, the model can predict adverse events with good performance and therefore, can be regarded as a gatekeeper before patients with sepsis are admitted to the general ward.
keywords: Deep learning;Explainability;Sepsis;Mortality;Adverse event

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Support: Present Implementations, Innovative Tools, and Research Horizons
journal: 2025 World Skills Conference on Universal Data Analytics and Sciences (WorldSUAS)
authors: Y. Joshi and N. Gupta and D. Mishra
abstract: Over the last decade, the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) within mental healthcare has expanded rapidly, emerging as a potential response to both the increasing demand for psychiatric care and the shortage of qualified professionals. This review synthesises based on recent evidence (2019–2025) exploring applications of AI in mental health care, concentrating on screening, diagnosis, intervention delivery, monitoring, and explainable AI (XAI) practices. Comprehensive coverage was pursued by applying a systematic and predefined search strategy across relevant sources by using major databases such as IEEE Xplore, PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, incorporating both clinical evidence and technical contributions. Artificial intelligence methods including natural language processing, acoustic analysis, visual recognition, and multimodal fusion are increasingly utilised for both clinical applications and preventive mental health interventions. Commercial tools and research prototypes are reviewed within three categories: chatbot-based therapy and triage, emotional well-being applications, and "smart" mental health tools for diagnostics and monitoring. While these technologies show promise in improving access, scalability, and personalisation, persistent challenges include limited long-term evidence, algorithmic bias, privacy concerns, lack of empathy, trustworthiness, and the need for culturally adaptive systems. Explainable-AI (XAI) emerges as a critical enabler for trust, transparency, and safe adoption, especially in high-stakes mental health decisions and support. Future research should prioritise large-scale, longitudinal trials, multimodal integration, and regulatory frameworks that align with rapid technical advances
keywords: Artificial Intelligence;Mental Health;Machine Learning;Explainable AI (XAI);Digital Therapeutics;Therapy

title: Integrating Deep Learning and Explainable AI for Non-Invasive Prediction of EGFR and KRAS Mutations in NSCLC: A Novel Radiogenomic Approach
journal: 2024 V International Conference on Neural Networks and Neurotechnologies (NeuroNT)
authors: F. Shariaty and V. A. Pavlov and S. V. Fedyashina and N. A. Serebrennikov
abstract: The diagnosis of lung cancer is based on phenotypic and genetic data, providing a foundation for the development of personalized treatment strategies. The integration of ExplainableAI (XAI) methods into the predictive modeling of gene mutations in lung cancer represents a pivotal advancement in theinterpretability and trustworthiness of deep learning algorithms. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) inconjunction with a ResNet18 model is employed to elucidate the features within lung nodule CT images that are indicative of specific genetic mutations, such as EGFR and KRAS. The XAI results, particularly the Grad-CAM heatmaps, serve as a bridge between the deep learning model's computational predictions and the clinical understanding of lung tumor morphology and its genetic underpinnings. This exploration not only enhances the explainability of AI models but also contributes to a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between morphological features and genetic variations, potentially leading to more targeted and personalized treatments for lung cancer patients.
keywords: Lung cancer;XAI;Deep Learning;KRAS;EGFR

title: Challenges and Opportunities in Quantum-Enhanced XAI for Medical and Healthcare Systems
journal: 2025 IEEE Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC)
authors: R. Cecere and A. Santopaolo and G. F. Russo and F. Iodice and V. S. Di Cola
abstract: Quantum technologies and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) present an exciting avenue for improving operating workflows, customizing therapies, and improving diagnostics. Quantumenhanced XAI has the potential to revolutionize healthcare systems and medicine, making it an important field for research. These developments allow doctors to make data-driven choices, eventually improving patient outcomes and raising the standard of care. The authors have focused their essays on these topics to spark insightful conversations and promote more research into the possible uses, difficulties, and future directions of hybrid quantum systems and XAI. The authors’ focus on Quantum-Enhanced XAI is to stimulate a discussion that offers fresh viewpoints and ideas, especially concerning developing methodologies, improving current approaches, and investigating creative applications in cutting-edge fields. Lastly, the authors provide suggestions for further study and useful advice for scholars and practitioners working in the medical and healthcare fields.
keywords: Quantum Computing;Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI);Medical Diagnostics;Healthcare Systems;Quantum Algorithms;Interpretability;Ethical AI

title: Explainable NLP Model for Predicting Patient Admissions at Emergency Department Using Triage Notes
journal: 2023 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (BigData)
authors: E. Arnaud and M. Elbattah and P. A. Moreno-Sánchez and G. Dequen and D. A. Ghazali
abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has the potential to revolutionize healthcare by providing more transparent, trustworthy, and understandable predictions made by AI models. To this end, the present study aims to develop an explainable NLP model for predicting patient admissions to the emergency department based on triage notes. We utilize transformer models to leverage the extensive textual data captured in triage notes, while also delivering interpretable results by using the LIME approach. The results show that the proposed model provides satisfactory accuracy along with an interpretable understanding of the factors contributing to patient admission. In general, this work highlights the potential of NLP in improving patient care and decision-making in emergency medicine.
keywords: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI);Natural Language Processing;BERT;Transformers;Emergency Department;Triage

title: Medico Assistant: An AI-Driven Real-Time Multi-Modal Triage System
journal: 2025 2nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Knowledge Discovery in Concurrent Engineering (ICECONF)
authors: P. J and J. C. P and G. Mahalakshmi
abstract: Lack of medical and human resources often leads to major issues in emergency triage, involving patients being prioritized incorrectly and the ED being cram-full. This research paper proposes implementing an AI-driven “Medico Assistant” to revolutionize the use of triage in EDs. The ongoing triage systems use static assessments, which may cause ineffective resource allocation and delayed actions. Our novel approach integrates the usage of real-time multi-modal data, including ambient sensor data, unstructured clinical notes, Electronic Health Records (EHR), and patient-reported symptoms, using a refined deep learning architecture. Furthermore, XAI will be used to furnish coherent explanations of its findings and personalized, frugal suggestions. By enhancing ET accuracy and efficacy, it enables early critical interventions and fast-track resource usage. This “Medico Assistant” gives way to improved patient outcomes in stretched clinical environments.
keywords: ED-Emergency Department;EHR-Electronic Health Records;Explainable AI (XAI)

title: Real-Time Multi-Class Brain Haemorrhage Detection with Visual Explanations using Grad-CAM
journal: 2025 3rd International Conference on Sustainable Computing and Smart Systems (ICSCSS)
authors: S. V. Ch and K. Pradha Rayavarapu and K. Komirishetty and R. Reddy and S. B. Pendam
abstract: Intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) is an emergent and potentially life-threatening diagnosis caused by intracranial or surrounding structure bleeding. Detection needs to be timely and correct to enhance outcomes in patients but is frequently impeded by radiologist shortages, limited time, and human error in high-pressure or low-resource environments. In order to overcome this challenge, we introduce a real-time, interpretable deep model based on the ResNet-50 architecture for multi-label classification of the five most common forms of brain hemorrhages: subdural, subarachnoid, intraventricular, intraparenchymal, and epidural. The model is trained on a balanced portion of the RSNA Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection dataset and makes use of sigmoid activation with binary cross-entropy loss to manage multiple labels per CT scan. To further the transparency and trustworthiness, we integrate Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping), which produces heatmaps demarcating regions of interest within the CT images that impacted the model's predictions. Such visual interpretability assists the clinicians in comprehending and validating the AI's outputs. Moreover, a light-weight Streamlit-based web interface enables users to upload scans and get on-the-fly predictions along with the respective Grad-CAM outputs. The system offers a useful, easy-to-use tool for supporting emergency triage and facilitating the use of explainable AI in radiological workflows.
keywords: brain hemorrhage;CT scan;multi-label classification;deep learning;ResNet-50;Grad-CAM;explainable AI;Streamlit interface

title: Improving Emergency Triage in Crisis Situations: a Hybrid GAN-Boosting Approach With Machine Learning
journal: 2025 IEEE Afro-Mediterranean Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AMCAI)
authors: A. ZIDI and I. Nouaouri and I. B. JAAFAR
abstract: Emergency departments (EDs) must quickly assess and prioritize patients, especially during crises when demand exceeds capacity. Traditional triage methods, such as the JumpSTART protocol for pediatric cases and the START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) method for adults, are commonly used but may lack precision under high-pressure situations. This paper proposes a hybrid approach combining ensemble models-XGBoost, AdaBoost, and CatBoost-with synthetic data augmentation using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to enhance triage accuracy for critically ill patients. Models were trained on real-world ED data, including vital signs, symptoms, medical history, and demographics. GANs generated synthetic critical cases to address class imbalance, improving model sensitivity to high-risk profiles. Results show that GAN-augmented models outperform baseline models, with CatBoost offering the best balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. This approach improves patient prioritization, reduces delays, and supports better clinical decision-making in resource-limited environments.
keywords: Emergency Department (ED);Patient Triage;Machine Learning (ML);AdaBoost;XGBoost;CatBoost;Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs);Urgency Classification;Crisis Situations

title: Sparse Embedding for Interpretable Hospital Admission Prediction
journal: 2019 41st Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC)
authors: Z. Huo and H. Sundararajhan and N. C. Hurley and A. Haimovich and R. A. Taylor and B. J. Mortazavi
abstract: This paper introduces a sparse embedding for electronic health record (EHR) data in order to predict hospital admission. We use a k-sparse autoencoder to embed the original registry data into a much lower dimension, with sparsity as a goal. Then, t-SNE is used to show the embedding of each patient's data in a 2D plot. We then demonstrate the predictive accuracy in different existing machine learning algorithms. Our sparse embedding performs competitively against the original data and traditional embedding vectors with an AUROC of 0.878. In addition, we demonstrate the expressive power of our sparse embedding, i.e. interpretability. Sparse embedding can discover more phenotypes in t-SNE visualization than original data or traditional embedding. The discovered phenotypes can be regarded as different risk groups, through which we can study the driving risk factors for each patient phenotype.

title: Multimodal AI for Chest Disease Diagnosis: Integrating Medical Imaging and Clinical Data
journal: 2026 3rd International Conference on Advancements and Key Challenges in Green Energy and Computing (AKGEC)
authors: V. Mishra and T. Gupta and V. Kumar and S. Sharma and R. Gupta
abstract: The chest disease is also sensitive and equitable in diagnosis, though it is a great battle in resource-poor practices in which expert radiological interpretation and complete laboratory support are not always available. But here are the most recent events. Variance in artificial intelligence (AI) would help connect different types of data, such as chest radiographs, basic clinical findings, and lab results, into useful automated diagnostic pipelines. This multimodal solution can be more predictive and clinically useful when each source of data utilizes its own advantage. Modern AI-based applications have been very good at making predictions about the severity of an illness, the needed treatments, and the outcome for the patient. and the scores for the area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC). Combining imaging, laboratory, and clinical data with a score of over 0.75. More importantly, the AI algorithms can surpass solo models and are interpretable by attributing features, which contributes to the triage of resources and decision-making by non-specialist practitioners. However, there are still issues concerning algorithmic biases, failure to diagnose underserved subpopulations, and the extrapolation of models on variable patients demographics and institutional settings. Safe and effective deployment must be thoroughly validated in the real-world clinical context, and equity of data represented and clear reports must be considered. The use of multimodal AI solutions has the potential to democratize the access to quality diagnostics of chest diseases in healthcare systems with limited resources, and, finally, health disparities and patient outcomes will be reduced.
keywords: multimodal AI;chest disease diagnosis;medical imaging;clinical data integration;interpretability;healthcare equity;resource-limited settings;algorithmic bias;AI validation

title: Exploring the Ethical Challenges of Large Language Models in Emergency Medicine: A Comparative International Review
journal: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
authors: M. Elbattah and E. Arnaud and D. A. Ghazali and G. Dequen
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) hold promise for advancing Emergency Medicine by enhancing operational efficiency and supporting decision-making. This scoping review explores the ethical, legal, and global considerations influencing LLM deployment in emergency care. Key ethical concerns, including patient safety, data privacy, and transparency, emphasise the need for explainable AI (XAI) to build trust and prevent biased outputs. Legal challenges highlight the importance of regulatory compliance, especially regarding data protection laws like the GDPR. Significant international variability in LLM adoption further underscores the need for harmonised guidelines to ensure safe and equitable AI integration across diverse healthcare systems. To advance the responsible use of LLMs, future research should prioritise model transparency, consider resource-limited settings, and focus on establishing robust regulatory frameworks.
keywords: Large Language Models;LLMs;Emergency Medicine;Emergency Department

title: Explainable AI for Medical Image Analysis in Medical Cyber-Physical Systems: Enhancing Transparency and Trustworthiness of IoMT
journal: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
authors: W. Liu and F. Zhao and A. Shankar and C. Maple and J. D. Peter and B. -G. Kim and A. Slowik and B. D. Parameshachari and J. Lv
abstract: This study explores the application of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in the context of medical image analysis within medical cyber-physical systems (MCPS) to enhance transparency and trustworthiness. Meanwhile, this study proposes an explainable framework that integrates machine learning and knowledge reasoning. The explainability of the model is realized when the framework evolution target feature results and reasoning results are the same and are relatively reliable. However, using these technologies also presents new challenges, including the need to ensure the security and privacy of patient data from Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). Therefore, attack detection is an essential aspect of MCPS security. For the MCPS model with only sensor attacks, the necessary and sufficient conditions for detecting attacks are given based on the definition of sparse observability. The corresponding attack detector and state estimator are designed by assuming that some IoMT sensors are under protection. It is expounded that the IoMT sensors under protection play an important role in improving the efficiency of attack detection and state estimation. The experimental results show that the XAI in the context of medical image analysis within MCPS improves the accuracy of lesion classification, effectively removes low-quality medical images, and realizes the explainability of recognition results. This helps doctors understand the logic of the system's decision-making and can choose whether to trust the results based on the explanation given by the framework.
keywords: Explainable artificial intelligence;medical image;medical cyber-physical systems;IoMT;sparse observability

title: XAI Driven Intelligent IoMT Secure Data Management Framework
journal: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
authors: W. Liu and F. Zhao and L. Nkenyereye and S. Rani and K. Li and J. Lv
abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has transformed traditional healthcare systems by enabling real-time monitoring, remote diagnostics, and data-driven treatment. However, security and privacy remain significant concerns for IoMT adoption due to the sensitive nature of medical data. Therefore, we propose an integrated framework leveraging blockchain and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to enable secure, intelligent, and transparent management of IoMT data. First, the traceability and tamper-proof of blockchain are used to realize the secure transaction of IoMT data, transforming the secure transaction of IoMT data into a two-stage Stackelberg game. The dual-chain architecture is used to ensure the security and privacy protection of the transaction. The main-chain manages regular IoMT data transactions, while the side-chain deals with data trading activities aimed at resale. Simultaneously, the perceptual hash technology is used to realize data rights confirmation, which maximally protects the rights and interests of each participant in the transaction. Subsequently, medical time-series data is modeled using bidirectional simple recurrent units to detect anomalies and cyberthreats accurately while overcoming vanishing gradients. Lastly, an adversarial sample generation method based on local interpretable model-agnostic explanations is provided to evaluate, secure, and improve the anomaly detection model, as well as to make it more explainable and resilient to possible adversarial attacks. Simulation results are provided to illustrate the high performance of the integrated secure data management framework leveraging blockchain and XAI, compared with the benchmarks.
keywords: Explainable artificial intelligence;Internet of Medical Things (IoMT);secure data management;blockchain;bidirectional simple recurrent unit;local interpretable model-agnostic explanations

title: Deep Learning in Healthcare
journal: 2025 2nd International Conference on Integration of Computational Intelligent System (ICICIS)
authors: A. Kumar and A. Tewary and A. Raj and Shruti and P. K. Samanta
abstract: Deep learning is reshaping healthcare across medical imaging, clinical text, time-series physiology, and genomics. This review synthesizes methods and applications with emphasis on model families (CNN/UNet/ViT; RNN/Transformers), datasets and evaluation practices (AUROC/AUPRC, Dice, calibration, external validation). We summarize benefits—earlier detection, consistent triage and personalized decision support—alongside persistent challenges including data quality and shift, fairness, interpretability, privacy and regulatory alignment. To support responsible translation, we propose a practical evaluation checklist covering robustness, calibration, subgroup performance and workflow integration. We conclude with near-term research priorities: self-supervised and federated learning for data efficiency and privacy, multimodal modeling for holistic patient state and prospective validation with post-deployment monitoring. This synthesis aims to guide researchers and practitioners toward clinically credible, trustworthy AI systems.
keywords: Deep Learning;Healthcare;Medical Imaging;Clinical Text;Physiological Signals;Genomics;Responsible AI

title: Decompensation Prediction for Hospitalized COVID-19 Patients
journal: 2022 IEEE 10th International Conference on Healthcare Informatics (ICHI)
authors: M. Singh and J. Liu and L. Kirkland and J. Srivastava
abstract: Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, hospitals have been overwhelmed with the high number of ill and critically ill patients. The surge in ICU demand led to ICU wards running at full capacity, with no signs of demand falling. As a result, resource management of ICU beds and ventilators has been a bottleneck in providing adequate healthcare to those in need. Short-term ICU demand forecasts have become a critical tool for hospital administrators. Therefore, using the existing COVID-19 patient data, we build models to predict if a patient's health will deteriorate below safe thresholds to deem admission into ICU in the next 24 to 96 hours. We identify the most important clinical features responsible for the prediction and narrow down the health indicators to focus on, thereby assisting the hospital staff in increasing responsiveness. These models can help the hospital staff better forecast ICU demand in near real-time and triage patients for ICU admissions as per the risk of deterioration. Using a retrospective study with a dataset of 1411 COVID-19 patients from an actual hospital in the USA, we run experiments and find XGBoost performs the best among the models tested when tuning parameters for sensitivity (recall). The most important feature for the four prediction tasks is the maximum respiratory rate, but subsequent features in order of importance vary between models predicting ICU transfer in the next 24 to 48 hours and those predicting ICU transfer in the next 72 to 96 hours.
keywords: patient deterioration;feature importance;XG-Boost;supervised machine learning;COVID-19

title: Explainable AI-Enabled Wearable Sensors for Real-Time Thrombotic Event Early Warning in Connected Health Environments
authors: Z. Wang and Y. Hu and Q. Hu and D. Bai
abstract: Thrombotic events have multiple complications that remain difficult to identify early unless continuous non-invasive monitoring solutions are available to consumers; however, developing such products has been very restrictive thus far. In this article we provide an overview about a novel Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) framework for wearable sensors and the earliest warning systems for thrombotic events in a connect health environment. Our framework is dedicated to supporting integration with mainstream consumer wearable technologies (smartwatches, fitness trackers) and allows for ease of implementation in existing consumer electronics ecosystems whilst still achieving clinical-grade prediction accuracy. We developed a method that integrates multimodal physiological signals from ECG-derived heart rate variability (HRV) as well as dynamics of skin temperature into a hierarchical attention based model that provides risk assessments that are interpretable and clinically relevant; Our extensive experiments show that the predictive accuracy of ThrombXAI is at 91.3% using an AUC value of 0.936 and represents improvements of 4.2% and 2.8% respectively to the current best available state-of-the-art methods for thrombotic event prediction. We further validated our results in a prospective study on 156 participants and compared the results to traditional screening approaches, in which we discovered statistically significant improvements; 89.3% sensitivity and 91.5% specificity for the early identification of thrombotic events. We provide the way forward with new paradigms of personalized preventative cardiovascular medicine using consumer wearables integrated with clinically actionable XAI technology.
keywords: Explainable artificial intelligence;wearable sensors;thrombotic event prediction;deep learning;connected health;edge computing;attention mechanisms;clinical decision support

title: Call2Care: Real-Time Voice and Call Recording-Based Symptom-to-Disease Diagnosis
journal: 2026 5th International Conference on Innovative Practices in Technology and Management (ICIPTM)
authors: U. Mishra and S. Rai and S. Tyagi and V. Raj and D. Devi
abstract: The given paper presents a new system known as Call2Care to attempt to automate preliminary medical triage through voice and call recordings in real-time. The framework integrates advanced speech recognition, natural language processing to transcribe patient conversations (NLP), and machine learning are used, symptomatic information to be extracted, formatted, and anticipated likely types of disease. Known to be developed to work hard when used in noisy telephonic conditions, the system will overcome issues like fluctuating audio quality, regional accents and non-technical patient vocabulary. We checked our system with fake doctor calls and real voice recordings from people. During the tests, it was able to correctly find the main symptoms and predict the right illness about 86 percent of the time. The paper outlines the system architecture, which puts an increased emphasis on interpretability and privacy, and its potential to provide healthcare access to distant and underserved population as a decision-support tool to the human operators.
keywords: Speech Recognition;Natural Language Processing;Symptom Extraction;Disease Prediction;Telemedicine;Clinical Triage

title: Early Risk Prediction for Emergency Department Triage using Machine Learning Techniques
journal: 2026 International Conference on AI-Driven Smart Systems and Ubiquitous Computing (ICAUC)
authors: B. Lalithadevi and J. S. Prasanna and J. S. Sri
abstract: The Emergency departments are concerned with major challenges such Crowding, waiting times, and sometimes irrational triage can be observed in many crisis or emergency departments. In this regard, this article introduces an automated Predictive Triage and Queue Management System using machine learning algorithms that predicts patient severity and prioritizes patient treatment delivery. To this end, this system utilizes gradient boosting algorithms XGBoost and LightGBM. To establish the efficacy and efficiency of this system, Random Forest classification has been used as the baseline model for performance comparisons. Based on patient vital signs and symptoms, patient predictive classification results in immediate output for priority-based patient queuing for effective crisis or emergency treatment. To measure the efficiency and effectiveness of this approach, results show that boosting algorithms outperform the baseline models by providing improved patient classification accuracy, precision, and F1-score performance. To provide additional interpretation and improvements in doctor-patient communication and understanding for effective treatment, SHAP-based interpretability has been implemented in this system. For an enhanced and more effective system with improved functionality, several extensions need to be implemented in the future. These extensions would include automated vital patient monitoring and integrating this system with EHRs (Electronic Health Record system services)
keywords: Emergency Department;Triage;Machine Learning;Queue Management;SHAP Explainability

title: Explainable Machine Learning-Based Analysis for Identifying Risk Factors of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
journal: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Digital Health (ICDH)
authors: C. Jayanath and E. Arnaud and M. Elbattah
abstract: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a major global health issue. Early detection and identification of risk factors are critical for effective management. This study applies explainable machine learning techniques using LIME and SHAP to analyze a large US dataset and provide interpretable insights into COPD risk factors. While established factors such as smoking and age remain central, the analysis also highlights the underappreciated influence of mental health, physical inactivity, and comorbid conditions. These insights enable a more holistic understanding of COPD risk profiles and support the development of tailored prevention strategies. While limited to US data, the findings pave the way for future studies incorporating diverse populations
keywords: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease;COPD;Explainable Machine Learning;XAI

title: Dual Ontology-enhanced Clinical Decision Learning for First-admission Mortality Prediction
journal: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
authors: F. Yin and H. Nie and X. Pu and P. Zheng and Q. Zhu and Y. Ren and L. Deng
abstract: Time-series based deep learning methods have significantly improved performance of predictive healthcare tasks on electronic health records (EHR) data. However, mortality prediction for first admissions is a huge challenge due to the absence of historical visit sequences. Analysis of major healthcare databases reveals that 55.17% in MIMIC-IV and 83.80% in MIMIC-III present with single visit records only. Many of these single-visit patients are admitted directly to ICU, highlighting the critical need for early prediction models that can inform timely interventions and substantially impact patient outcomes, even without longitudinal history. On first-admission mortality prediction, Dual Ontology-enhanced Clinical Decision learning (DOCD) has been proposed in this paper where we effectively leverage clinical knowledge through two key components. Dual ontology-enhanced learning extracts hierarchical representations from both diagnosis and procedure taxonomies. Furthermore, a priori-guided attention mechanism integrates clinical knowledge through probability based regularization to model the decision-making process. An information fusion is then employed to seamlessly integrate the demographic data, vital signs, and knowledge enhanced medical codes. Extensive experiments on MIMIC III (AUROC: 0.9528, AUPRC: 0.8971) and MIMIC-IV (AUROC: 0.9817, AUPRC: 0.8857) datasets demonstrate DOCD's superior performance over all baselines, offering interpretable visualizations aligned with established clinical knowledge.
keywords: Electronic Health Records;First Admission;In-hospital Mortality;Medical Ontology Representa tion;A Priori-guided Attention;Model Interpretability

title: PLEX: Perturbation-Free Local Explanations for LLM-Based Text Classification
journal: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing
authors: Y. Rahulamathavan and M. Farooq and V. De Silva
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in text classification, but their complexity hinders interpretability, making it difficult to understand the reasoning behind their predictions. Explainable AI (XAI) methods like LIME and SHAP offer local explanations by identifying influential words, but they rely on computationally expensive perturbations. These methods typically generate thousands of perturbed sentences and perform inferences on each, incurring a substantial computational burden, especially with LLMs. To address this, we propose Perturbation-free Local Explanation (PLEX), a novel method that leverages the contextual embeddings extracted from the LLM and a “Siamese network” style neural network trained to align with feature importance scores. This one-off training eliminates the need for subsequent perturbations, enabling efficient explanations for any new sentence. We demonstrate PLEX's effectiveness on four different classification tasks (sentiment, fake news, fake COVID-19 news and depression), showing more than 92% agreement with LIME and SHAP. Our evaluation using a “stress test” reveals that PLEX accurately identifies influential words, leading to a similar decline in classification accuracy as observed with LIME and SHAP when these words are removed. Notably, in some cases, PLEX demonstrates superior performance in capturing the impact of key features. PLEX dramatically accelerates explanation, reducing time and computational overhead by two and four orders of magnitude, respectively. This work offers a promising solution for explainable LLM-based text classification.
keywords: Explainable AI;LIME;SHAP;LLM;BERT;text classification

title: Machine Learning Models Predict Fatal Myocardial Infarction Within 10-Years Follow-Up Utilizing Explainable AI
journal: 2023 IEEE 23rd International Conference on Bioinformatics and Bioengineering (BIBE)
authors: K. -H. Tsarapatsani and A. Sakellarios and V. D. Tsakanikas and M. Kleber and W. Marz and D. I. Fotiadis
abstract: Fatal myocardial infarction (MI) is one of the most common types of cardiovascular diseases that often presents in the emergency department. The prediction of death caused by myocardial infarction within 10-years follow-up is addressed in this study, using comorbidities, daily habits, clinical and laboratory data in binary and continuous data respectively. The used data are included in a cohort of the Ludwigshafen Risk and Cardiovascular Health (LURIC) study. The target feature, namely death caused by MI, contained 106 deceased patients and 2,321 alive patients in the final used dataset. The analysis was based on machine learning models (ML), such as support vector machine (SVM), light gradient-boosting machine (LGBM), Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT). Their performance was estimated by Area Under Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC), Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision and Accuracy. Results show that LGBM was the most suitable of the aforementioned models to predict death caused by myocardial infarction within 10-years follow-up, achieving area under the curve (AUC) value equal to 77.03 %, accuracy 69.42 %, sensitivity 69.75 %, specificity 69.40% and precision 53.76 %. In addition, explainable artificial intelligence (xAI) was utilized and especially SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was the selected method. SHAP was utilized in order to shed light on the results, applying the LGBM model as the best predictive model. The provided SHAP plots contribute to the interpretation of how each independent feature aid to the final prediction.
keywords: machine learning;myocardial infarction;explainable AI

title: Explainable Profiling of Sleep Disorders to Support Trustworthy Clinical Interventions
journal: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining Workshops (ICDMW)
authors: S. Sellami and J. Agoun and L. Yessad and A. Berro and L. Bounia
abstract: Sleep disorders present significant diagnostic challenges due to symptom heterogeneity, profoundly impacting public health. To address this, we leverage real-world data from the KANOPEE mobile application-a validated digital tool for managing sleep complaints-to develop a trustworthy model for disorder detection and patient profiling using explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Guided by clinical expertise, our analysis focuses on key variables including demographic characteristics, clinical assessment scores (e.g., Insomnia Severity Index, anxiety, and depression scores), and physiological metrics. Our dataset comprises approximately $1 k$ complete patient records. Our dual methodological approach involves: (1) regression models to predict treatment success metrics, enabling the identification of modifiable behavioral factors influencing mental health and sleep outcomes; and (2) k-means clustering to segment patients into three or more distinct profiles, differentiating subtypes of sleepers (e.g., young professionals with mild insomnia and anxiety, older individuals with regular sleep and low depression, and middle-aged patients with high daytime sleepiness and irregular sleep patterns). XAI techniques, including SHAP and formal explanations, elucidate key drivers like sleep regularity and anxiety, validated against clinical thresholds and expert feedback from sleep specialists. This framework aligns algorithmic insights with medical reasoning, enhancing interpretability and supporting personalized interventions in digital sleep medicine. Future extensions will incorporate application completion rates for broader efficacy assessment.
keywords: Sleep Disorder Profiling;Explainable AI (XAI);K-means Clustering;Inter-Cluster Statistical Analysis;RealWorld Data Analysis

title: Predicting 30-Day All-Cause Hospital Readmission Using Multimodal Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks
journal: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
authors: S. Tang and A. Tariq and J. A. Dunnmon and U. Sharma and P. Elugunti and D. L. Rubin and B. N. Patel and I. Banerjee
abstract: Reduction in 30-day readmission rate is an important quality factor for hospitals as it can reduce the overall cost of care and improve patient post-discharge outcomes. While deep-learning-based studies have shown promising empirical results, several limitations exist in prior models for hospital readmission prediction, such as: (a) only patients with certain conditions are considered, (b) do not leverage data temporality, (c) individual admissions are assumed independent of each other, which ignores patient similarity, (d) limited to single modality or single center data. In this study, we propose a multimodal, spatiotemporal graph neural network (MM-STGNN) for prediction of 30-day all-cause hospital readmission, which fuses in-patient multimodal, longitudinal data and models patient similarity using a graph. Using longitudinal chest radiographs and electronic health records from two independent centers, we show that MM-STGNN achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.79 on both datasets. Furthermore, MM-STGNN significantly outperformed the current clinical reference standard, LACE+ (AUROC = 0.61), on the internal dataset. For subset populations of patients with heart disease, our model significantly outperformed baselines, such as gradient-boosting and Long Short-Term Memory models (e.g., AUROC improved by 3.7 points in patients with heart disease). Qualitative interpretability analysis indicated that while patients' primary diagnoses were not explicitly used to train the model, features crucial for model prediction may reflect patients' diagnoses. Our model could be utilized as an additional clinical decision aid during discharge disposition and triaging high-risk patients for closer post-discharge follow-up for potential preventive measures.
keywords: Graph neural network;multimodal fusion;hospital readmission prediction;chest radiographs

title: Machine Learning in Healthcare: Transforming Patient Outcome Prediction and Decision Support
journal: 2025 2nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence for Innovations in Healthcare Industries (ICAIIHI)
authors: A. Shrivastava and S. O. Husain and A. Bhansali and A. Yadav and G. Maurya and A. Dutt
abstract: This review integrates evidence from 24 pivotal studies investigating the application of machine learning (ML) towards predicting clinical outcomes across various healthcare environments. Literature is shown to indicate that ML methods are highly effective at improving the predictability of patient outcomes relative to conventional models. Applications span from emergency department triage and sepsis identification to psychiatric evaluation and postoperative recovery, integrating templated data like electronic health records, administrative claims, imaging, and patient-reported outcomes. Supervised learning models—most prominently gradient boosting, random forests, and neural networks—prevail in outcome prediction tasks, with increasing interest in causal ML methods for treatment effect estimation. Multiple studies emphasize ML's potential to provide timely and individualized insights, supporting early intervention and enhancing decision-making. Despite positive findings, interpretability, generalizability, data quality, and workflow integration still pose challenges. Rigorous validation, ethical handling of data, and explainable models are highlighted throughout the literature. Finally, ML has the power to transform predictive healthcare by facilitating timely, data-informed, and patient-oriented care delivery.
keywords: machine learning;clinical outcome prediction;patient-reported outcomes;healthcare analytics;electronic health records;predictive modeling

title: MediHealth AI: An Integrated Framework for Automated Health Report Analysis, Symptom Triage, and Conversational Assistance
journal: 2025 7th International Conference on Innovative Data Communication Technologies and Application (ICIDCA)
authors: D. Kawde and C. Puri
abstract: The surging popularity of health information on the Web and the current lack of healthcare specialists in the world have made it necessary to develop not only clever, but also self-governing health systems. The current paper presents a new product based on the integrated artificial intelligence platform, named MediHealth AI, with the ability to optimize the delivery of healthcare through three functionalities, including self-sustaining health report analysis, intelligent symptom triaging, and interactive patient communication. Through Natural Language Processing (NLP), Machine Learning (ML), and Explainable AI (XAI), the platform provides actionable intelligence of both structured and unstructured healthcare data, lists with the symptomary severity of the patients, and live suggestions and recommendations on an interactive chatbot interface. The potential of the MediHealth AI is unfathomable when it comes to optimizing the clinical workload, diagnostic effectiveness, and providing an individual with the necessary data on their health they need and at the opportune time. Substantiated by literature and supported experimentally, there is great increased accuracy of diagnosis and patient satisfaction. The framework overcomes the existing issues of mismanagement of clinical data related to information overload, interoperability, and fairness of algorithms in AI-driven applications and introduces scalable, transparent, and human-centered digital health.
keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI);Natural Language Processing (NLP);Machine Learning (ML);Symptom Triage;Health Report Analysis;Conversational AI;Clinical Decision Support

title: Deep Learning for Detection and Localization of B-Lines in Lung Ultrasound
journal: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
authors: R. T. Lucassen and M. H. Jafari and N. M. Duggan and N. Jowkar and A. Mehrtash and C. Fischetti and D. Bernier and K. Prentice and E. P. Duhaime and M. Jin and P. Abolmaesumi and F. G. Heslinga and M. Veta and M. A. Duran-Mendicuti and S. Frisken and P. B. Shyn and A. J. Golby and E. Boyer and W. M. Wells and A. J. Goldsmith and T. Kapur
abstract: Lung ultrasound (LUS) is an important imaging modality used by emergency physicians to assess pulmonary congestion at the patient bedside. B-line artifacts in LUS videos are key findings associated with pulmonary congestion. Not only can the interpretation of LUS be challenging for novice operators, but visual quantification of B-lines remains subject to observer variability. In this work, we investigate the strengths and weaknesses of multiple deep learning approaches for automated B-line detection and localization in LUS videos. We curate and publish, BEDLUS, a new ultrasound dataset comprising 1,419 videos from 113 patients with a total of 15,755 expert-annotated B-lines. Based on this dataset, we present a benchmark of established deep learning methods applied to the task of B-line detection.
