To pave the way for interpretable quantification of B-lines, we propose a novel “single-point” approach to B-line localization using only the point of origin. Our results show that (a) the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranges from 0.864 to 0.955 for the benchmarked detection methods, (b) within this range, the best performance is achieved by models that leverage multiple successive frames as input, and (c) the proposed single-point approach for B-line localization reaches an F$_{1}$-score of 0.65, performing on par with the inter-observer agreement. The dataset and developed methods can facilitate further biomedical research on automated interpretation of lung ultrasound with the potential to expand the clinical utility.
keywords: Lung ultrasound;B-lines;deep learning;COVID-19;heart failure

title: A Review of CAM-Based Visual Explanation on Diabetic Retinopathy
authors: A. Galang Persada and I. Ardiyanto and M. Bayu Sasongko and H. A. Nugroho
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide, and deep learning systems have achieved competitive performance for DR screening. However, the lack of transparent visual explanations remains a barrier to clinical adoption. Class Activation Map (CAM) methods are widely used to visualize model attention on fundus images, yet their behavior, evaluation, and clinical validity in DR remain fragmented across the literature. We conducted a PRISMA-ScR–guided scoping review of CAM-based visual explanation methods applied to DR classification and lesion-level analysis on color fundus photographs. We searched PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, and arXiv from 2016 to 2024, using combinations of keywords related to “diabetic retinopathy”, “class activation map”, and “explainable AI”. Studies were included if they applied CAM-family techniques to DR grading or lesion detection on retinal fundus images. The results are a total of 28 studies that met our criteria, covering 14 public and private datasets, predominantly EyePACS, Messidor, APTOS, IDRiD, and FGADR. We summarize the use of Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, Score-CAM, Ablation-CAM, LayerCAM, and several DR-specific CAM variants across common backbones (e.g., ResNet, EfficientNet, DenseNet) and categorize evaluation metrics into pixel- and lesion-level localization (IoU, Dice, DAUC/IAUC, ADD, DC/IC, ADCC) and causal faithfulness. We identify recurrent failure modes such as vessel-focused heatmaps, optic disc glare, and poor sensitivity to low-contrast microaneurysms. This review provides an evidence map of CAM-based explanations in DR, highlights gaps between visual plausibility and causal faithfulness, and proposes a compact “what works when” guideline relating DR task, dataset, backbone, and CAM choice. We present a clinical validity lens for lesion-level fidelity and referable DR triage, along with practical recommendations for standardized evaluation and clinically grounded CAM development in DR.
keywords: Diabetic retinopathy;explainable AI;class activation map;medical imaging

title: Video Summarization and Fracture Detection in Pediatric Wrist Ultrasound Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
journal: 2025 47th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC)
authors: S. Ghosh and G. Vadali and Y. Zhou and A. Singh and J. Knight and C. Keen and M. R. Panicker and A. R. Hareendranathan and J. L. Jaremko
abstract: Wrist fractures are common injuries among children, significantly impacting daily activities and contributing to prolonged wait times in emergency departments. Portable ultrasound is a safe, radiation-free, and cost-effective diagnostic tool with real-time imaging capabilities to identify these fractures. Ultrasound (US) videos offer dynamic, detailed views for fracture detection but can be lengthy and redundant, making interpretation time-consuming for clinicians. To address this challenge, we developed a novel video summarization and fracture detection method using Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). The DRL agent emulates a human expert by analyzing the entire video, selecting diagnostically relevant frames, and leveraging a CNN to classify these frames as either normal or fractured. The reward mechanism, which prioritizes feature similarity and frame dissimilarity, enhances the agent’s ability to identify the keyframes. Anisotropic diffusion is applied to US images to enhance bright bony regions, before feature extraction and representativeness calculation. Frame similarity calculations are parallelized to reduce computational complexity, storage demands and simplify the classification task by focusing solely on frames indicative of fractures. On a dataset of 114 patients, the proposed classification network achieved an accuracy of 88.8% with a sensitivity of 92.5% and a specificity of 86.6% using the RL-generated video summaries. Our primary focus is on enhancing sensitivity to ensure that no fractured cases are missed. This performance surpasses the 84.4% accuracy achieved with full video classification. AI-driven ultrasound, with its efficiency, and reduced computational demands, provides a promising solution for early disease detection in resource-constrained environments.Clinical relevance— This AI-driven fast, cost-effective ultrasound tool achieves high accuracy and sensitivity while reducing training time by 50%, making it suitable for real-time clinical use on low-power devices. This can assist lightly-trained healthcare providers in early disease detection, reduce long wait times, and enhance treatment access in remote areas.
keywords: Wrist ultrasound;fracture detection;video;summarization;RL;CNN;segmentation;classification

title: Automated Risk Assessment of COVID-19 Patients at Diagnosis Using Electronic Healthcare Records
journal: 2021 IEEE EMBS International Conference on Biomedical and Health Informatics (BHI)
authors: F. O. Giuste and L. L. He and M. Isgut and W. Shi and B. J. Anderson and M. D. Wang
abstract: COVID-19 causes significant morbidity and mortality and early intervention is key to minimizing deadly complications. Available treatments, such as monoclonal antibody therapy, may limit complications, but only when given soon after symptom onset. Unfortunately, these treatments are often expensive, in limited supply, require administration within a hospital setting, and should be given before the onset of severe symptoms. These challenges have created the need for early triage of patients likely to develop life-threatening complications. To meet this need, we developed an automated patient risk assessment model using a real-world hospital system dataset with over 17,000 COVID-positive patients. Specifically, for each COVID-positive patient, we generate a separate risk score for each of four clinical outcomes including death within 30 days, mechanical ventilator use, ICU admission, and any catastrophic event (a superset of dangerous outcomes). We hypothesized that a deep learning binary classification approach can generate these four risk scores from electronic healthcare records data at the time of diagnosis. Our approach achieves significant performance on the four tasks with an area under receiver operating curve (AUROC) for any catastrophic outcome, death within 30 days, ventilator use, and ICU admission of 86.7%, 88.2%, 86.2%, and 87.8%, respectively. In addition, we visualize the sensitivity and specificity of these risk scores to allow clinicians to customize their usage within different clinical outcomes. We believe this work fulfills a clear clinical need for early detection of objective clinical outcomes and can be used for early screening for treatment intervention.

title: EventScore: An Automated Real-time Early Warning Score for Clinical Events
journal: 2022 IEEE 10th International Conference on Healthcare Informatics (ICHI)
authors: I. Hammoud and P. Prasanna and I. Ramakrishnan and A. Singer and M. Henry and H. Thode
abstract: Early prediction of patients at risk of clinical deterioration can help physicians intervene and alter their clinical course towards better outcomes. In addition to the accuracy requirement, early warning systems must make the predictions early enough to give physicians enough time to intervene. Interpretability is also one of the challenges when building such systems since being able to justify the reasoning behind model decisions is desirable in clinical practice. In this work, we built an interpretable model for the early prediction of various adverse clinical events indicative of clinical deterioration. The model is evaluated on two datasets and four clinical events. The first dataset is collected in a predominantly COVID-19 positive population at Stony Brook Hospital. The second dataset is the MIMIC III dataset. The model was trained to provide early warning scores for ventilation, ICU transfer, and mortality prediction tasks on the Stony Brook Hospital dataset and to predict mortality and the need for vasopressors on the MIMIC III dataset. Our model first separates each feature into multiple ranges and then uses logistic regression with lasso penalization to select the subset of ranges for each feature. The model training is completely automated and doesn't require expert knowledge like other early warning scores. We compare our model to the Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) and quick SOFA (qSOFA), commonly used in hospitals. We show that our model outperforms these models in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) while having a similar or better median detection time on all clinical events, even when using fewer features. Unlike MEWS and qSOFA, our model can be entirely automated without requiring any manually recorded features. We also show that discretization improves model performance by comparing our model to a baseline logistic regression model.
keywords: Machine Learning;Electronic Health Records;Early Warning Score;eOVID-19;Event Prediction;Healthcare;Hospitals;Electronic Medical Records;MIMIC Dataset;Early Event Prediction;Interpretable Machine Learning

title: Explainable Tuberculosis Detection from Chest X-Rays Using SHAP-Pruned CNN Features and Gradient-Boosted Classification
journal: 2025 IEEE 6th Global Conference for Advancement in Technology (GCAT)
authors: B. Tiwari
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) detection from chest radiographs requires models that balance predictive accuracy with transparent decision-making. This study introduces an explainable pipeline combining deep convolutional feature extraction with SHAP-based feature pruning, followed by gradient-boosted classification. Preprocessed lung-masked X-rays from the TBX11K (Simplified) dataset were used, with training and testing performed on a stratified 80/20 split. Global and local SHAP values guided the elimination of non-informative descriptors, while Grad-CAM attention maps were evaluated against ground-truth bounding boxes using Intersection-over-Union (IoU) and Dice metrics to quantify spatial fidelity. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves robust performance (Accuracy: 95.6%, AUROC: 0.969) and consistently surpasses both CNN and CNN+XGBoost baselines. Reliability was further assessed using Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier score, ensuring well-calibrated probability outputs for threshold-sensitive clinical decisions. Confusion matrix analysis highlighted common failure modes, such as subtle apical opacities, while sensitivity checks on pruning thresholds confirmed the model’s robustness. The findings indicate that SHAP-guided feature selection improves both predictive efficiency and interpretability, offering a reproducible and clinically aligned approach for TB triage using chest radiographs.
keywords: Classification;Explainability;Grad-CAM;SHAP;Tuberculosis;X-ray

title: TeleXAI-R: A Real-Time Explainable AI Model for Remote Patient Risk Stratification Using IoT-Integrated Consumer Devices
authors: J. Yang and J. Dai and X. Tang and M. A. Khan and M. Ayadi and Z. A. Shaikh and A. Alasiry and M. Marzougui and P. Su and L. Y. Por
abstract: Remote patient monitoring (RPM) via smart consumer electronics is revolutionizing post-discharge and chronic disease management. Yet, current AI-powered RPM systems often lack transparency, adaptability across diverse devices, and integration into clinical triage systems. To address this, we introduce TeleXAI-R, an explainable AI-driven risk stratification model that operates in real-time across IoT-integrated consumer devices such as pulse oximeters, blood pressure monitors, and smart rings. TeleXAI-R incorporates a transformer-based temporal encoder for dynamic vital sign prediction and an XAI attention module that visualizes feature importance over time. We develop a cloud-edge hybrid inference engine to enable on-device alerts and clinician dashboards. The model also includes a confidence-aware alerting system to reduce false positives in high-noise settings. Core contributions include: 1) a temporal interpretability framework tailored for RPM; 2) cross-device calibration and data standardization protocol; and 3) integration with FHIR-compatible clinical workflows. Experiments on a real-world dataset of 1,200 patients show 90.1% precision in early risk detection for cardiac events, while maintaining interpretability that clinicians rated 4.7/5 in a usability study. TeleXAI-R sets the foundation for trustworthy RPM in connected healthcare. Unlike prior temporal-attention pipelines, TeleXAI-R couples a rhythm-aware transformer with a calibrated, device-agnostic alignment layer and a confidence-adaptive alerting mechanism that jointly optimize latency, interpretability, and false alerts. Removing any of these core components leads to significant drops in precision and F1, underscoring their necessity.
keywords: Explainable AI;remote patient monitoring;IoT healthcare;risk stratification;consumer electronics

title: ADAM-1: An AI Reasoning and Bioinformatics Model for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection and Microbiome-Clinical Data Integration
authors: Z. Huang and V. Kaur Sekhon and R. Sadeghian and M. L. Vaida and C. Jo and B. A. McCormick and D. V. Ward and V. Bucci and J. P. Haran
abstract: Alzheimer’s Disease Analysis Model Generation 1 (ADAM-1) is a multi-agent reasoning large language model (LLM) framework designed to integrate and analyze multimodal data, including microbiome profiles, clinical datasets, and external knowledge bases, to enhance the understanding and classification of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). By leveraging the agentic system with LLM, ADAM-1 produces insights from diverse data sources and contextualizes the findings with literature-driven evidence. A comparative evaluation with XGBoost revealed a significantly improved mean F1 score and significantly reduced variance for ADAM-1, highlighting its robustness and consistency, particularly when utilizing human biological data. Although currently tailored for binary classification tasks with two data modalities, future iterations will aim to incorporate additional data types, such as neuroimaging and peripheral biomarkers, and expand them to predict disease progression, thereby broadening ADAM-1’s scalability and applicability in AD research and diagnostic applications.
keywords: Alzheimer’s disease;artificial intelligence;multi-agent systems;knowledge based systems

title: Explainable AI for Automated Emergency Triage of Brain CT Pathologies: A Multi-Level Classification Framework
journal: 2026 International Conference on AI Innovations and Industry (ICAIII)
authors: K. Aljuaid and H. Meshref
abstract: The quick and accurate distinction between intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) and ischemic stroke is very important for emergency neurological triage since these diseases necessitate treatments that are totally opposite from each other. The present study gives a detailed deep learning framework for automated brain CT pathology classification which is tested on three complementary case studies. We performed a thorough comparison of traditional machine learning (XGBoost, Random Forest, SVM, Logistic Regression) versus state-of-the-art deep learning architectures (EfficientNet-B0/B7, ResNet18/50/152, DenseNet121, ConvNeXt-Large, Swin Transformer) using 8,097-13,500 CT images classified into seven hemorrhage categories (Normal, Ischemia, Intraventricular, Intraparenchymal, Subarachnoid, Epidural, Subdural). In Case Study 1, EfficientNet-B0 accomplished seven-class accuracy of $90.33\%}$ with $4.0M$ parameters, surpassing traditional ML by 17.79 percentage points. In Case Study 2, three-window CT preprocessing (Brain/Subdural/Bone windows) was applied with ensemble stacking achieving clinical-grade 97.26% four-class accuracy. In Case Study 3, a near-perfect 99.21% three-class accuracy was reached through Swin Transformer-based voting ensemble. Explainable AI integration (Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, LIME) confirmed that the models accurately concentrated on the sites of hemorrhage and ischemia, thus excluding artifacts. The real-time inference $(<20 ~\text{ms}$ per image) makes it suitable for emergency situations. The findings prove that the triaging process can be fully automated for neurological emergencies, which need very quick human-like expert-level decisions.
keywords: Brain CT;XAI;intracranial hemorrhage;LIME Ischemia;Strokes;Deep learning;Grad-CAM;Swin transformer

title: Enhanced Tuberculosis Detection using a Dual-Path Vision Model with Feature-Space Augmentation and Progressive Fine-Tuning
journal: 2025 IEEE 17th International Conference on Computational Intelligence and Communication Networks (CICN)
authors: T. V and M. N. Devi and S. K and S. B
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health threat, necessitating rapid and accurate diagnostic tools. Conventional Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation is often hampered by resource constraints and human variability. This paper presents DPVM-MS (Dual-Path Vision Model with Mirage Synthesizer), a novel hybrid architecture for pulmonary tuberculosis (PB) detection from chest radiography (CXR) images, that integrates both ResNet50 for local image features and ViT-Base Transformer for the global context in the image via Multihead Attention mechanism. The architecture was deliberately designed to enhance generalization and regularization by introducing the novel Mirage Synthesizer (MS), a learnable and perturbatively designed feature-space augmentation module, along with a stabilizing Progressive Fine-Tuning (PFT) regimen. The evaluation included strict patient-wise stratification and cross-dataset validation across four cohorts: Shenzhen (N=662) and Montgomery (N=138) and DATASET A (N=156) and DATASET B (N=122) (from the National Institute of Tuberculosis and Respiratory Diseases, New Delhi). DPVM-MS achieved high validation accuracies of 90.62% to 96.00% and significantly outperformed the single-path baselines; and for balanced generalization, it achieved perfect Specificity (1.0000) in DATASET B and perfect Sensitivity (1.0000) in the Montgomery dataset, which demonstrated it was a highly accurate and robust positioning it as a resilient diagnostic tool suitable for WHO screening and triage recommendations in low-resource settings.
keywords: Tuberculosis (TB);Chest X-ray (CXR);Hybrid Vision Model;Mirage Synthesizer;Multihead Attention;Progressive Fine-Tuning

title: Cardiovascular Disease Risk Prediction Model Based on Fast-Tunable Optimized Stacked Ensemble Learning Architecture
journal: 2025 7th International Academic Exchange Conference on Science and Technology Innovation (IAECST)
authors: F. Cui and X. Li and Y. Wu and W. Chen and D. Kong and J. Li and X. Liu and C. Du
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is one of the leading causes of global mortality and disability. Early identification and risk prediction of CVD are crucial for its prevention and effective clinical management. This study proposes a CVD risk prediction model based on the Fast-Tunable Optimized Stacked Ensemble Learning (FT-OSEL) architecture. Building upon the original Optimized Stacked Ensemble Learning (OSEL) framework, FT-OSEL integrates lightweight network structures, adaptive fine-tuning mechanisms, parallel training strategies leveraging task-level parallelism, and knowledge distillation techniques, achieving significant improvements in training speed, prediction accuracy, and fine-tunability. The proposed model enables interpretable risk factor analysis and probabilistic predictions through temperature-scaled knowledge distillation, where the original OSEL serves as the teacher model and FT-OSEL as the student model. It further integrates established interpretability techniques—SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME)—to enhance transparency. Cross-dataset validation on an independent external cohort confirms its generalization capability. Experimental results indicate that FT-OSEL not only surpasses conventional approaches but also improves upon the original OSEL architecture, offering a more efficient and interpretable solution for early CVD screening.
keywords: Cardiovascular disease;Ensemble learning;Stacked ensemble;Bayesian optimization;Knowledge distillation

title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Framework for ICU Mortality Risk Prediction in COVID-19 Patients
journal: 2026 6th International Conference on Image Processing and Capsule Networks (ICIPCN)
authors: R. Ingole and D. Moharle and V. Mahalle and A. Bangade and R. Rewatkar
abstract: It is critically important to have dependable tools available to help identify inpatients during admission for those patients at highest risk for in-hospital death due to COVID19. The COVID19 Pandemic has created an unprecedented amount of demand on intensive care units (ICUs) around the world; consequently, it is vital to initiate clinical intervention and allocate limited intensive care unit (ICU) resources as quickly as possible by early risk stratification among patients, particularly in an intensive care unit (ICU) setting. This article combines routinely-collected clinical data routinely available at the time of admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) in order to provide a predictive analytic framework for evaluating the mortality of patients who have been admitted into an intensive care unit (ICU) due to COVID19 infection. The final data set consisted of 1,250 patients admitted into the intensive care unit (ICU) from a tertiary care medical center, of these patients, approximately 28% had died as a direct result of their COVID infection. A variety of supervised learning techniques were tested including, Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosting Machines, Extra Trees, XGboost, and Random Forests; Frequently loaded datasets from Methodological Evaluation were used as the source for developing and validating the supervised machine learning models listed above. The Random Forest Model selected as the Optimal Classifier Model had excellent classification capabilities and inherent interpretable features. The Random Forest classifier model had an ROC-AUC of 0.866, an F1 of 0.566, and a Recall of 0.439 when evaluated on a holdout Test Dataset; Features considered important for predicting clinical outcomes consistent with adapting clinical management based on current clinical knowledge were: Age, Oxygen Saturation Levels, Inflammatory Markers, and Comorbidities. In light of the fact that moderate recall highlights the potential for false negative results, the framework should be viewed as a means to aid clinical judgement rather than replace it. Overall, the proposed strategy provides an open, evidence-based decision support system for use in ICU triage and resource allocation during pandemics.
keywords: COVID-19;clinical data;interpretable AI;machine learning;ICU mortality prediction;risk stratification

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Early Assessment of COVID-19 Risk Prediction in Emergency Departments
authors: E. Casiraghi and D. Malchiodi and G. Trucco and M. Frasca and L. Cappelletti and T. Fontana and A. A. Esposito and E. Avola and A. Jachetti and J. Reese and A. Rizzi and P. N. Robinson and G. Valentini
abstract: Between January and October of 2020, the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) virus has infected more than 34 million persons in a worldwide pandemic leading to over one million deaths worldwide (data from the Johns Hopkins University). Since the virus begun to spread, emergency departments were busy with COVID-19 patients for whom a quick decision regarding in- or outpatient care was required. The virus can cause characteristic abnormalities in chest radiographs (CXR), but, due to the low sensitivity of CXR, additional variables and criteria are needed to accurately predict risk. Here, we describe a computerized system primarily aimed at extracting the most relevant radiological, clinical, and laboratory variables for improving patient risk prediction, and secondarily at presenting an explainable machine learning system, which may provide simple decision criteria to be used by clinicians as a support for assessing patient risk. To achieve robust and reliable variable selection, Boruta and Random Forest (RF) are combined in a 10-fold cross-validation scheme to produce a variable importance estimate not biased by the presence of surrogates. The most important variables are then selected to train a RF classifier, whose rules may be extracted, simplified, and pruned to finally build an associative tree, particularly appealing for its simplicity. Results show that the radiological score automatically computed through a neural network is highly correlated with the score computed by radiologists, and that laboratory variables, together with the number of comorbidities, aid risk prediction. The prediction performance of our approach was compared to that that of generalized linear models and shown to be effective and robust. The proposed machine learning-based computational system can be easily deployed and used in emergency departments for rapid and accurate risk prediction in COVID-19 patients.
keywords: Associative tree;Boruta feature selection;clinical data analysis;COVID-19;generalized linear models;missing data imputation;random forest classifier;risk prediction

title: Predicting Avoidable Emergency Department Visits Using the NHAMCS Dataset
journal: 2021 IEEE 9th International Conference on Healthcare Informatics (ICHI)
authors: S. Liu and J. Yu and Y. Yang
abstract: Avoidable emergency department (ED) visits contribute increased costs to the healthcare system and lead to overcrowding that can limit capacity to treat patients. There has been little work to develop models from patient characteristics that can predict avoidable ED visits. Here we apply machine learning methods using the NHAMCS dataset to predict avoidable ED visits and identify patient characteristics associated with avoidable ED.
keywords: Emergency Care;Machine Learning;Healthcare Utilization

title: ViT-ResNet Contrastive Adaptation for Pneumonia Detection
journal: 2025 8th International Conference on Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (BDAI)
authors: T. Wang and J. Zou and L. Shi and J. Liu
abstract: Pneumonia remains a major global health challenge requiring reliable diagnostic solutions. Current chest X-ray analysis faces limitations due to variability across radiologists and imaging protocols. This study develops a hybrid vision transformer and ResNet architecture with contrastive domain adaptation, combining global context learning and localized feature extraction while improving out-of-sample generalization. A clinical integration module fuses C-reactive protein levels and patient age, improving specificity relative to the image-only model. Validation on 5863 pediatric chest X-rays from Guangzhou Maternal and Child Medical Center achieved an AUC 0.970 (95 \% CI 0.963-0.977) and an accuracy of 91.7\%. Incorporating C-reactive-protein and age features raised specificity from 89% to $93 \%(+4.0 \mathrm{pp})$ over the image-only baseline, while visual explanations reached 89% pixel-level agreement with radiologist annotations. Although the current study relies on a single-center cohort, the proposed framework offers a transparent and readily deployable solution for pneumonia triage in resource-limited settings.
keywords: Pneumonia detection;domain adaptation;vision transformers;explainable AI

title: Emergency Department Forecasting: COVID-19 Impact on Machine Learning Models
journal: 2025 IEEE CHILEAN Conference on Electrical, Electronics Engineering, Information and Communication Technologies (CHILECON)
authors: A. S. López and H. Álvarez-Chaves and A. C. Fernández and M. D. R-Moreno
abstract: COVID-19 disrupted emergency department (ED) arrival patterns, creating challenges for traditional forecasting models used in hospital resource planning. This study analyzes ED arrival data from two Spanish hospitals to assess how the pandemic period affects Machine Learning (ML) model performance and identify optimal forecasting strategies. We applied multiple ML techniques (XGBoost, Random Forest, Elastic Net) and timeseries algorithms (ARIMA, Prophet) using both daily and work shift temporal aggregations, incorporating exogenous calendar variables, including holidays and academic schedules. Models were trained on pandemic-inclusive and post-pandemic periods to evaluate the impact of including disrupted historical data. Results demonstrate that models trained exclusively on postpandemic data consistently outperform those including pandemic data, achieving R2 improvements of up to 0.13 for 4-month forecasts. Work shift aggregation significantly enhanced performance compared to daily aggregation (R2 = 0. 9 2 vs 0. 6 4 for best models). SHAP analysis revealed that recent patient arrivals and calendarrelated features serve as the most important predictors across all scenarios. These findings indicate that excluding pandemic data from training datasets and employing finer temporal aggregation substantially improve ED arrival forecasting accuracy, providing practical benefits for hospital operations and resource allocation.
keywords: COVID;Forecasting;Time Series;Emergency Department;Machine Learning;Exogenous Variables;SHAP

title: Machine Learning-based Stroke Detection using CT and MRI Imaging
journal: 2026 9th International Conference on Inventive Computation Technologies (ICICT)
authors: H. R and R. M and S. K and S. S
abstract: Differentiating between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke is important, as both are major causes of death and disability. With the development of medical imaging, machine learning (ML) is also applied to stroke detection and triage. This work focuses on recent advances in the machine learning methods used for stroke detection that appeared from 2020 till 2025 in CT/MRI images. In this work, we analyze and compare the evolution of deep-learning-based architectures, such as CNN, U-Net, transformers, and hybrid ensembles, from classical classifiers with handcrafted modalities. This review is based on how to categorize lesion types, localize hemorrhage, and isolate ischemic infarctions, as well as combined imaging strategies. Some recent advances like transfer learning, low-power CNNs for edge applications, uncertainty-aware ideas, and explainable AI for improved clinical interpretation are also discussed. But there still exist many challenges, including domain shifts across scanners, multi-center validation limited in scale, interpretability lacking in a model, and easy association with patient records under the privacy constraint. This review details methodological advancements and unresolved challenges associated with the above-mentioned methodologies. We view the ability to recognize strokes with ML as a key enabler that can help emerging needs like real-time, robust, and equitable diagnostic support systems toward ultimately beginning to deploy AI in acute stroke management.
keywords: stroke detection;updated algorithm;medical imaging;deep learning;performance evaluation;explainable AI;future scope

title: Reinforcement Learning for Intelligent Healthcare Systems: Optimizing Patient Treatment and Resource Allocation in Dynamic Clinical Environments
authors: R. Joshi and K. Pandey and S. Kumari and A. Bharti and M. Mohanty and D. Upadhyay
abstract: This study presents a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for optimizing intelligent decision-making policies in dynamic, domain-agnostic environments. Unlike traditional rule-based systems, RL agents adapt to uncertainty, learn from interaction, and converge toward efficient strategies over time. We implement and evaluate Deep Q-Network (DQN) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) using real-data-inspired benchmarks, measuring performance through cumulative rewards, policy entropy, action distribution, convergence stability, and sample efficiency. The results demonstrate PPO's superior learning stability and faster convergence compared to DQN. Baseline data visualizations, such as triage delay patterns and severity-linked outcomes, provide reference points to highlight how RL outperforms static protocols. These evaluations confirm that RL is wellsuited for scalable, real-time decision automation, offering a reliable alternative where traditional systems are limited by rigidity and inefficiency. The proposed approach sets a foundation for deploying RL in complex, adaptive control scenarios.
keywords: Reinforcement Learning;Intelligent Healthcare;Patient Treatment Optimization;Resource Allocation;Emergency Department Triage;Drug Dosage Optimization;AI in Healthcare;Deep Q-Networks;Proximal Policy Optimization;Hospital Staffing;Healthcare Cost;Optimization;Machine Learning

title: Explainable AI Chatbot for Animal Behavioral and Medical Triage
journal: 2026 4th International Conference on Intelligent Data Communication Technologies and Internet of Things (IDCIoT)
authors: D. P and H. B. R and P. R
abstract: An understanding of animal behavior is critical for not only animal welfare reasons but for purposes of risk factor prevention, as well as human interaction. However, in trying to make sense out of their behavior, actions, emotions, and intentions, specialized knowledge is required in most instances, hence leaving most pet owners in the dark concerning what particular behavior means. It is proposed: Explainable AI Chatbot for Animal Behavioral and Medical Triage. It integrates a multimodal behavior-understanding pipeline that combines vision-based action recognition with pose estimation and contextaware reasoning models for inference of the underlying causes driving such behaviors as aggression, fear, restlessness, abnormal posture, social signaling, or environmental responses. To foster trust and usability, the system embeds an explainability module able to generate human-readable reasoning that explains “why the animal performed this action” by highlighting visual cues, movement patterns, or contextual features relevant to the prediction. And in the case of unusual, distressing, or pathological behavior, a structured medical triage dialogue is started, with specific questions to decide if veterinary attention could be required. It uses light veterinary knowledge models for screening purposes and also conveys the level of uncertainty while not offering any diagnoses that fall outside the realm of the chat bot. It offers insight on how explainable multimodal AI can close the communication divide between human beings and animals through scientific behavioral interpretation. Based on the work performed within this paper, the research on explainable animalcentric AIs has just begun.
keywords: multimodal behavior;action recognition;explainability;human-readable reasoning;veterinary attention;behavioral interpretation

title: Implementation and Testing of an Experimental Near-Real-Time Patient Bedside Monitor Datastream Analysis and Alerting System in a Live Emergency Department
journal: 2024 IEEE 15th Annual Ubiquitous Computing, Electronics & Mobile Communication Conference (UEMCON)
authors: L. Kobayashi and A. Oyalowo and U. Agrawal and S. -L. Chen and J. W. Gosbee and X. Hu and K. A. Loparo and G. D. Jay and D. L. Merck
abstract: Academic emergency physicians and data scientists collaborated on a research program to reduce false alarms and to increase the utility of patient monitor systems for detecting significant cardiopulmonary events and clinical deterioration. An experimental hardware-software framework to study patient monitoring and alarm fatigue mitigation was implemented in 15 Emergency Department (ED) urgent care spaces of a regional medical center. Patients who triggered multi-parametric alerts [MPA] consisting of two or more red alarms (critical cardiac rhythm, heart rate [HR], blood pressure [BP], or oxygen saturation) within a 15-minute window were consented and matched into 1:1:1 study triads with patients who only triggered standard, single parameter (red) alarms [SPA] and those who remained in a non-alarm state [NA]. Study patients’ red alarms and triggering physiologic abnormalities (vital signs; cardiac rhythm and pulse oximetry photoplethysmography waveforms) were adjudicated and annotated for validity (chart review) and interpretability (clinician gestalt). Each subject was then followed for 3 months via in-network medical records. Subjects’ characteristics, alarms, clinical courses, and outcomes were descriptively and comparatively analyzed. The relationship between alarm-triggering waveform interpretability and alarm validity was analyzed with correlational statistics, along with the association between multi-parametric alerts and severity of patient state.Of 264 ED patients enrolled over 24 months, 183 matched into 61 triads matched for sex, age, Emergency Severity Index (ESI), and chief complaint; 27.1% of MPA, 10.9% of SPA, and 5.2% of NA subjects started care in ED critical care (X2(2)=6.47, p=0.04). MPA and SPA subjects triggered single parameter red alarms of all types, with a predominance of tachycardia and hypoxia alarms. Asystole and ventricular fibrillation/ventricular tachycardia (VFib/VTach) alarms were mostly adjudicated as non-valid, and hypoxia alarms were frequently of indeterminate validity, whereas HR and BP alarms were generally valid. Five (8.2%) MPA subjects and no SPA subjects (and no NA subjects) were transferred to ED critical care while monitored in the study area, X2(1)=9.41, p=0.002). Eleven (18.1%), five (8.2%), and two (3.3%) MPA, SPA, and NA subjects, respectively, were admitted from the ED to an intensive or intermediate care unit (p<0.001). Higher rates of symptomatic/unstable tachycardia (p=0.02) and post-ED escalation in care unit requirement (p=0.001) were recorded in MPA and SPA groups than in the NA group. Waveform interpretability scores in the 53 MPA subjects with complete data exhibited moderate positive correlation with the adjudicated validity of their red alarms, r(51)=0.528, p<0.001. The difference in composited 3-month tracer metrics between MPA and SPA groups did not attain statistical significance, although death (4.9%), Advanced Life Support (1.6%), and cardiac arrest (1.6%) were noted only in MPA patients.ED patient monitor datastreams were acquired and analyzed to explore novel biomedical engineering approaches to mitigate alarm fatigue. Safe experimentation in a live ED environment demonstrated the potential for near-real-time signals-level analysis of standard biomedical device outputs to differentiate true alarms from false alarms and to identify patients with a higher likelihood of poor outcomes.

title: Structural Self-Supervision for Label-Free Aortic Dissection Triage on Non-Contrast CT
journal: 2026 IEEE 23rd International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI)
authors: J. Lin and Z. Situ and G. Xie and W. Zhou
abstract: Effective triage of aortic abnormalities on non-contrast CT (NCCT) is critical for emergency care. Yet automated detection remains difficult due to low vessel–background contrast, resulting in unstable pseudo-segmentations and unreliable supervision. We address this by transforming pseudo-mask instability into a source of structural self-supervision. Instead of suppressing such variability, our framework leverages it to learn normative aortic anatomy and detect deviations indicative of pathology. It integrates three key modules: (1) Prompt-invariant Structural Embedding (PISE) enforces feature consistency across multiple SAM-based prompts; (2) Region-aware Disentanglement (RAD) isolates vessel-wall representations from surrounding tissues; (3) Consistency Evidence Map (CEM) provides transparent, radiologistaligned visualization of abnormal regions. On 363 multicenter NCCT scans, the proposed framework achieved an improvement of 0.056 in the Silhouette score, $\approx 45 \%$ lower representation variance, and AUROC $\approx 0.79$ for aortic dissection triage—outperforming unsupervised baselines and approaching expert-level interpretability. This study establishes a structural self-supervised paradigm that converts foundation-model uncertainty into structure-aware supervision, advancing interpretable, label-efficient, and scalable medical imaging AI for clinical deployment.
keywords: Structural self-supervision;non-contrast CT;aortic triage;interpretable AI

title: An Overview of Artificial Intelligence in Neuro-Oncology: Early Tumor Detection
journal: 2025 International Conference on Data, Energy and Communication Networks (DECoN)
authors: A. Gupta and P. Swami
abstract: The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methodologies has several novel opportunities such as earlier tumor detection, better surgical planning, and personalized care. The combination of new methods in the advanced imaging pipeline (pre-processing, segmentation, classification, and decision support) shows that convolutional, hybrid, and ensemble models have the ability to achieve more than 90 % accuracy on public MRI datasets. In some cases, AI models achieve close to $\text{1 0 0 \%}$ accuracy on small datasets through transfer learning and image fusion-based features. According to the review, AI application in neuro-oncological imaging delays diagnosis and thereby increases specialist availability and enables cost-effective triage, especially in underdeveloped areas. For effective AI benefits safe swallow, we emphasize certain prerequisites for clinical implementation, which include: privacy-preserving multi-center data sharing, an explainable AI to reveal solutions for the black-box opacity, strict external validation on heterogeneous populations and different scanners, and workforce/infrastructure preparedness (e.g., federated deployment, optimized protocol, and user training). The review finishes with recommendations and research gaps designed to address the challenges experienced with the implementation studies to provide fair, dependable, and wide-reaching care in neuro-oncology.
keywords: Neuro-oncology;meningiomas;gliomas;pathophysiology;imaging modalities

title: Development and Deployment of an Open, Modular, Near-Real-Time Patient Monitor Datastream Conduit Toolkit to Enable Healthcare Multimodal Data Fusion in a Live Emergency Department Setting for Experimental Bedside Clinical Informatics Research
authors: L. Kobayashi and A. Oyalowo and U. Agrawal and S. -L. Chen and W. Asaad and X. Hu and K. A. Loparo and G. D. Jay and D. L. Merck
abstract: Healthcare providers rely on complex biomedical devices to assess, treat, and monitor patients. Ongoing research efforts are attempting to generate and implement better algorithms and mechanisms to ensure the early, accurate, automated, and clinically meaningful recognition of patterns and changes in patient health and pathology. Effecting such evolutionary advances in patient monitoring will likely require large collections of high-resolution physiologic parameter datasets from a broad spectrum of patients. As part of a research program to scientifically improve patient monitoring (with a focus on alarm fatigue mitigation), investigators developed the Medical Technology Interface-Open/Research toolkit with modular conduit components that provide the following capabilities: 1) access to select bedside monitor physiologic signals in real-world clinical settings for near-real-time acquisition, storage, and export of high-resolution patient datastreams in a portable format (.json); 2) establishment of a safe, parallel test environment at the bedside for experimental datastream analyses in a research framework. Deployment and interfacing of toolkit elements with off-the-shelf software solutions in a live emergency department setting enabled the construction of a bedside clinical informatics (BCI) research pipeline infrastructure that featured 1) indexing, search/query, and retrieval of datastreams for sophisticated analyses, experimental processing, and algorithm development; and 2) dataset visualization for expert adjudication of datastream interpretability, alarm clinical significance and severity, and experimental algorithm performance. In order to help institute a collaborative biomedical engineering research resource, this article shares details of the active ED BCI data pipeline and presents preliminary examples of ongoing multimodal data fusion applications.
keywords: Alert fatigue health personnel;clinical alarms;information systems;medical informatics;patient-generated health data

title: Explainable Symptom-Based Chronic Disease Assessment Using Hybrid Rule-Based and Machine Learning Techniques
journal: 2026 5th International Conference on Innovative Practices in Technology and Management (ICIPTM)
authors: A. Verm and A. K. Dhuriya and O. Prakash
abstract: Online Symptom checkers provide quick, preliminary insights into potential health issues based on user-entered symptoms and data from medical wearable devices. These are gaining popularity worldwide because they empower self-assessment, guide triage decisions, and promote timely case-seeking; however, most existing systems rely on opaque, black-box machine learning or deep learning, or on rigid rule-based approaches, which undermine user trust and transparency. In this paper, we propose an explainable hybrid rule-based and machine learning model for the early detection of chronic diseases. Clinical rules, defined by experts and consisting of IF-THEN elements, are used to identify high-confidence, high-risk symptom patterns. In contrast, machine learning models are applied to the inference of complex or ambiguous instances. Let these symptom-based features and ambiguous instances be merged using hybrid fusion techniques and further classified using a machine learning classifier. The system prioritizes explainability by highlighting activated rules and clinical features for every decision. Two different clinical datasets have been selected for Experimental assessments: the first is the Heart Disease Cleveland dataset, and the second is the Chronic Kidney Disease dataset. These results suggested that the framework has the potential to provide accessible, reliable, symptom-based health advice at the initial stage.
keywords: Symptom Checker;Chronic Disease Assessment;Rule-Based System;Machine Learning;Explainable AI

title: A new machine learning technique for predicting traumatic injuries outcomes based on the vital signs
journal: 2019 25th International Conference on Automation and Computing (ICAC)
authors: F. Almaghrabi and D. -L. Xu and J. -B. Yang
abstract: Traditional vital signs are an essential part of triage assessment in emergency departments (ED), and have been widely used in trauma prediction models. Previous researchers have studied the effect of vital signs scores on predicting traumatic injury outcomes and have found it to be significant. Based on the vital signs’ scores, an Interpretable Machine Learning (IML) method is proposed to predict patient outcomes and is compared with various ML algorithms. Results indicate that the IML method has a comparable performance with a mean AUC of 0.683, and its interpretability would help in the early identification of trauma patients at risk of mortality.
keywords: Trauma outcome prediction;Interpretable machine learning technique;Vital signs;Belief rule-based inference;Maximum likelihood evidential reasoning

title: Predicting Patient Discharge Disposition in Acute Neurological Care
journal: 2021 IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (SSCI)
authors: C. F. Mickle and D. Deb
abstract: Acute neurological complications are some of the leading causes of death and disability in the U.S. and the medical professionals that treat patients in this setting are tasked with deciding where (e.g., home or facility), how, and when to discharge these patients. It is important to be able to predict ahead of time these potential patient discharge outcomes and to know what factors influence the development of discharge planning for such adults receiving care for neurological conditions in an acute setting. The goal of this study is to develop predictive models exploring which patient characteristics and clinical variables significantly influence discharge planning with the hope that the models can be used in a suggestive context to help guide healthcare providers in efforts of planning effective, equitable discharge recommendations. Our methodology centers around building and training five different machine learning models followed by testing and tuning those models to find the best-suited predictor with a dataset of 5,245 adult patients with neurological conditions taken from the eICU-CRD database. The results of this study show XGBoost to be the most effective model for predicting between four common discharge outcomes of ‘home’, ‘nursing facility’, ‘rehab’, and ‘death’, with 71% average c-statistic. This research also explores the accuracy, reliability, and interpretability of the best performing model by identifying and analyzing the features that are most impactful to the predictions.
keywords: machine learning;discharge planning;explainability;neurological

title: PathFinder: A Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System for Medical Diagnostic Decision-Making Applied to Histopathology
journal: 2025 IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
authors: F. Ghezloo and M. S. Seyfioglu and R. Soraki and W. O. Ikezogwo and B. Li and T. Vivekanandan and J. G. Elmore and R. Krishna and L. Shapiro
abstract: Diagnosing diseases through histopathology whole slide images (WSIs) is fundamental in modern pathology but is challenged by the gigapixel scale and complexity of WSIs. Trained histopathologists overcome this challenge by navigating the WSI, looking for relevant patches, taking notes, and compiling them to produce a final holistic diagnostic. Traditional AI approaches, such as multiple instance learning and transformer-based models, fail short of such a holistic, iterative, multi-scale diagnostic procedure, limiting their adoption in the real-world. We introduce PathFinder, a multi-modal, multi-agent framework that emulates the decision-making process of expert pathologists. PathFinder integrates four AI agents—the Triage Agent, Navigation Agent, Description Agent, and Diagnosis Agent—that collaboratively navigate WSIs, gather evidence, and provide comprehensive diagnoses with natural language explanations. The Triage Agent classifies the WSI as benign or risky; if risky, the Navigation and Description Agents iteratively focus on significant regions, generating importance maps and descriptive insights of sampled patches. Finally, the Diagnosis Agent synthesizes the findings to determine the patient's diagnostic classification. Our Experiments show that PathFinder outperforms state-of-the-art methods in skin melanoma diagnosis by 8% while offering inherent explainability through natural language descriptions of diagnostically relevant patches. Qualitative analysis by pathologists shows that the Description Agent's outputs are of high quality and comparable to GPT4o. PathFinder is also the first AI-based system to surpass the average performance of pathologists in this challenging melanoma classification task by 9%, setting a new record for efficient, accurate, and interpretable AI-assisted diagnostics in pathology. Data, code and models are available at https://pathfinder-dx.github.io/.
keywords: digital pathology;diagnostic ai;multi-agent systems;multimodal learning;vision-language models

title: Artificial Intelligence in Demand and Capacity Modelling of Healthcare Systems
journal: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
authors: C. Ribeiro and Y. Fan and C. Mullins and S. Williamson and J. Beard and P. Kourtessis and I. Mporas
abstract: The increasing complexity of healthcare systems management requires the development of advanced methodologies to support efficient resource allocation, service delivery, and strategic planning. Artificial intelligence has emerged as an important tool in this domain, offering capabilities to model demand, predict capacity requirements, and inform operational decisions through data-driven insights. This article provides a comprehensive scoping review of AI-based approaches for demand and capacity modelling in healthcare systems. Specifically, it examines AI methods applied to key demand prediction tasks, including outpatient activity, emergency department attendances, hospital admissions and readmissions, and length of stay, as well as capacity planning for beds, workforce, equipment, and other critical resources. The review reports trends in AI models design, learning paradigms, performance reporting, and data usage, and highlights the relationship between demand modelling and downstream capacity predictions. In addition, the paper analyses data infrastructure requirements, commonly used datasets, and the growing role of explainable AI in supporting transparency and trust. Despite recent advances in the field, the integration of AI into healthcare systems faces significant challenges, including concerns related to privacy, ethics, data quality, interpretability, bias, scalability, policy variation, and data interoperability. Addressing these challenges is essential to develop sustainable, fair and resilient healthcare systems. Our review highlights the current state and gaps in the literature, and proposes future directions for advancing the use of AI in healthcare management systems are reviewed.
keywords: Artificial Intelligence;Explainable AI;Machine Learning;Healthcare Management;Healthcare Demand Prediction;Healthcare Capacity Planning;Healthcare Operations Management;Medical Services

title: Cross-Regional and Interpretable Marine Mucilage Monitoring Using Spectral Indices and SHAP
authors: F. Yardımcı and Ç. Esi and A. Ertürk
abstract: The recurring phenomenon of marine mucilage in the Mediterranean region highlights the urgent need for effective environmental monitoring of marine ecosystems under stress. This study leverages Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery and incorporates a wide range of spectral indices to develop a CNN-based classification model for marine mucilage detection and mapping. The model was trained and validated on data of the Sea of Marmara, acquired in 2021, and tested on data from the Adriatic Sea, acquired in August 10, 2024, to evaluate its generalizability across geographically distinct regions. A SHAP-based explainability analysis was employed to assess the contributions of individual spectral indices to model predictions. The results highlight the robustness of key indices in mucilage detection and reveal new insights into their applicability across diverse environmental contexts, providing a foundation for broader monitoring applications in the Mediterranean.
keywords: Environmental monitoring;eXplainable Artifi-cial Intelligence (XAI);marine mucilage;spectral indices;SHap-ley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)

title: AI-Driven Assistance for Rapid Dermatology Triage
journal: 2025 3rd International Conference on Intelligent Cyber Physical Systems and Internet of Things (ICoICI)
authors: G. Sowmya and N. Jayasree and V. Chaithanya and T. Meena and B. U. Ranni and G. Aishwarya
abstract: Long waiting times for dermatology consultations significantly impact patient satisfaction and treatment outcomes, particularly for severe conditions requiring urgent care. This work presents SkinAI: Virtual Dermatology Assistant for Triage Acceleration, an AI-driven system leveraging computer vision and deep learning to analyze images of skin conditions uploaded by patients. The system determines the urgency level of each case and prioritizes severe conditions for immediate attention, thereby optimizing resource allocation in dermatology clinics. Continuous training on diverse and updated datasets enables SkinAI to identify a wide range of skin diseases accurately, accommodating variations in skin tones and conditions. By providing rapid and precise preliminary assessments, the system empowers dermatologists to focus on critical cases, reduces waiting times, and enhances overall healthcare efficiency. Initial evaluations demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy and sensitivity for urgent cases, underscoring the potential of SkinAI to improve patient outcomes and transform dermatological practice
keywords: Triage Recommendation;Skin condition;Patient satisfaction;Dermatology;image Recognition Introduction

title: Transfer Learning for Automated COVID-19 B-Line Classification in Lung Ultrasound
journal: 2022 44th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine & Biology Society (EMBC)
authors: J. R. Pare and L. A. Gjesteby and B. A. Telfer and M. M. Tonelli and M. M. Leo and E. Billatos and J. Scalera and L. J. Brattain
abstract: Lung ultrasound (LUS) as a diagnostic tool is gaining support for its role in the diagnosis and management of COVID-19 and a number of other lung pathologies. B-lines are a predominant feature in COVID-19, however LUS requires a skilled clinician to interpret findings. To facilitate the interpretation, our main objective was to develop automated methods to classify B-lines as pathologic vs. normal. We developed transfer learning models based on ResNet networks to classify B-lines as pathologic (at least 3 B-lines per lung field) vs. normal using COVID-19 LUS data. Assessment of B-line severity on a 0–4 multi-class scale was also explored. For binary B-line classification, at the frame-level, all ResNet models pretrained with ImageNet yielded higher performance than the baseline nonpretrained ResNet-18. Pretrained ResNet-18 has the best Equal Error Rate (EER) of 9.1% vs the baseline of 11.9%. At the clip-level, all pretrained network models resulted in better Cohen's kappa agreement (linear-weighted) and clip score accuracy, with the pretrained ResNet-18 having the best Cohen's kappa of 0.815 [95% CI: 0.804-0.826], and ResNet-101 the best clip scoring accuracy of 93.6%. Similar results were shown for multi-class scoring, where pretrained network models outperformed the baseline model. A class activation map is also presented to guide clinicians in interpreting LUS findings. Future work aims to further improve the multi-class assessment for severity of B-lines with a more diverse LUS dataset.

title: Multiclass Eye Disease Classification on Fundus Images Using EfficientNet-B3 and Grad-CAM
journal: 2025 International Conference on Computer Engineering, Network and Intelligent Multimedia (CENIM)
authors: A. P. Ramadhani and T. A. Sardjono and E. A. Suprayitno and N. F. Hikmah
abstract: Eye diseases such as Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), Glaucoma, and Cataract are among the main causes of global blindness, making early detection crucial to prevent irreversible retinal impairment. However, the manual evaluation of fundus images by ophthalmologists continues to be the primary diagnostic approach, limited by the availability of human resources, particularly in rural or disadvantaged areas. This study introduces an automated multi-class classification system for eye diseases using a deep learning model based on the EfficientNetB3 architecture, supported by Grad-CAM visualization to improve model interpretability. The system was trained using the Ocular Disease Intelligent Recognition (ODIR) dataset, which was categorized into five classes, including Normal, Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), Glaucoma, Cataract, and Other Diseases, the which has been simplified to only contain Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD). Pre-processing includes Circular Border Cropping, RGB Channel Extraction, CLAHE, Median Filtering, resizing to $300 \times 300$ pixels, and data augmentation. The model included pretrained ImageNet weights and was fine-tuned on the last $\mathbf{1 0 0}$ layers with a learning rate of $1 \mathrm{e}-6$ and a dropout rate of 0.3. The proposed model achieved a training accuracy of 97.08%, a validation accuracy of 87.20%, and a testing accuracy of 89.26%. These results indicate significant potential for medical application. The model can assist with triage or function as diagnostic tool in teleophthalmology and radiology processes. Future study may explore the application of other deep learning architectures and varied datasets to improve classification accuracy. Furthermore, combining additional imaging modalities beyond fundus images could expand the system’s application and improve diagnostic reliability.
keywords: CNN;Eye Disease;Fundus Image;Grad-CAM;Multi-class Classification

title: Explainable Intelligent Multi-Feature Fusion BTB Model for Teleconsultation in 6G-Enabled Healthcare Systems
authors: V. S. Kumar and A. Kollu and R. Avacharmal and P. S. Pandey and M. Kameswara Rao and A. Sundaram and E. Muniyandy
abstract: To address reliance on manual triage in current teleconsultation platforms, we propose a BTB intelligent triage model that supports next-generation 6G healthcare systems by integrating multi-feature fusion and Explainable AI (XAI) techniques. Assuming that the assigned consultation department in the dataset represents the optimal choice, the model uses patient age, gender, and preliminary diagnoses from primary care physicians to recommend appropriate specialty departments. To capture both local textual features and contextual dependencies in unstructured teleconsultation application records, the model combines BERT-based word embeddings, Text Convolutional Neural Network (TextCNN), and a double-layer Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) network. The extracted features are fused and passed through a fully connected layer to output a ranked list of recommended departments. The model was trained and validated on large-scale data from the National Telemedicine Center. When recommending the top five departments, it achieved an accuracy of 90.77% and a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of 76.45%. Moreover, the incorporation of explainability enables clinicians and patients to understand the rationale behind AI-driven recommendations, fostering trust and transparency. Experimental comparisons confirm that the proposed model significantly outperforms traditional machine learning approaches, offering a robust and interpretable solution for intelligent triage in teleconsultation-based consumer healthcare platforms.

title: AI and IoT-Integrated Smart Devices for Enhanced Vision Screening and Diagnosis in Eye Care
journal: 2024 2nd International Conference on Signal Processing, Communication, Power and Embedded System (SCOPES)
authors: S. Mereddy and S. Polaki and A. K. M and M. Ch and P. M. K and S. D
abstract: This study explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) in optometry for enhanced vision screening and diagnosis. Using IoT-enabled smart devices and AI models, including a convolutional neural network (CNN), the system achieved a 95.6% accuracy in classifying retinal diseases. SHAP analysis provided interpretability, with refractive error emerging as the most influential feature in visual acuity classification. Real-time monitoring enabled continuous assessment of visual parameters, triggering automated alerts for early intervention. Clinical validation showed high sensitivity (93.2%) and specificity (91.7%), while a user satisfaction score of 4.5 out of 5 indicated patient acceptance. The AI-IoT integrated system offers a scalable solution for proactive eye care, facilitating early diagnosis and personalized management. Future research will focus on integrating advanced diagnostics and expanding tele-optometry services to improve accessibility and effectiveness in diverse healthcare settings.
keywords: Smart Eye Care;AI in Vision Screening;IoT-Enabled Eye Care;Retinal Disease Classification;Real-Time Visual Monitoring

title: Advances and Challenges in AI-Powered Medical Chatbots: Leveraging LLMs, CNNs, and Multimodal Systems for Clinical Applications
journal: 2025 3rd DMIHER International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare, Education and Industry (IDICAIHEI)
authors: N. Pardhi and S. Hajare and T. Chute and A. S and N. Agade and D. Timande
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered medical chatbots are emerging as transformative tools in healthcare, offering capabilities that range from patient triage and diagnostic assistance to chronic disease management and medical education. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and multimodal architectures have significantly enhanced their ability to process complex medical data and deliver contextually accurate, patient-specific responses. This paper critically examines 26 recent works, with a focused analysis of ten primary studies, to evaluate the methodologies, performance metrics, and clinical applicability of state-of-the-art medical chatbot systems. The review highlights models such as MiniGPT-Med, ECG-Chat, MediGPT, and CNN-LSTM hybrids, which achieved accuracies exceeding 90% in specific diagnostic tasks, while also identifying limitations related to dataset diversity, interpretability, and real-world validation. The discussion underscores key challenges, including regulatory compliance, privacy preservation, and integration into existing clinical workflows. By synthesizing cross-disciplinary insights, this paper provides a consolidated view of current progress, critical gaps, and strategic directions necessary to enable safe, ethical, and scalable deployment of AI-based medical chatbots in global healthcare systems.
keywords: Artificial intelligence;medical chatbots;large language models;convolutional neural networks;multimodal AI;clinical decision support

title: Testing the Generalizability of an Automated Method for Explaining Machine Learning Predictions on Asthma Patients’ Asthma Hospital Visits to an Academic Healthcare System
authors: Y. Tong and A. I. Messinger and G. Luo
abstract: Asthma puts a tremendous overhead on healthcare. To enable effective preventive care to improve outcomes in managing asthma, we recently created two machine learning models, one using University of Washington Medicine data and the other using Intermountain Healthcare data, to predict asthma hospital visits in the next 12 months in asthma patients. As is common in machine learning, neither model supplies explanations for its predictions. To tackle this interpretability issue of black-box models, we developed an automated method to produce rule-style explanations for any machine learning model's predictions made on imbalanced tabular data and to recommend customized interventions without lowering the prediction accuracy. Our method exhibited good performance in explaining our Intermountain Healthcare model's predictions. Yet, it stays unknown how well our method generalizes to academic healthcare systems, whose patient composition differs from that of Intermountain Healthcare. This study evaluates our automated explaining method's generalizability to the academic healthcare system University of Washington Medicine on predicting asthma hospital visits. We did a secondary analysis on 82,888 University of Washington Medicine data instances of asthmatic adults between 2011 and 2018, using our method to explain our University of Washington Medicine model's predictions and to recommend customized interventions. Our results showed that for predicting asthma hospital visits, our automated explaining method had satisfactory generalizability to University of Washington Medicine. In particular, our method explained the predictions for 87.6% of the asthma patients whom our University of Washington Medicine model accurately predicted to experience asthma hospital visits in the next 12 months.
keywords: Asthma;automated explanation;extreme gradient boosting;machine learning;patient care management;predictive model

title: Multimodal Deep Learning for Pediatric Mild Traumatic Brain Injury Detection
journal: 2023 IEEE EMBS International Conference on Biomedical and Health Informatics (BHI)
authors: B. Mazumder and D. K. Tripathy and K. O. Yeates and M. H. Beauchamp and W. Craig and Q. Doan and S. B. Freedman and C. Lebel and R. Zemek and A. L. Ware and D. Hye Ye
abstract: Despite its prevalence, little is known about the pathophysiology of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). This makes it difficult for clinicians to accurately diagnose mTBI and to predict outcomes in affected children, thereby highlighting the urgent need to identify novel and efficacious biomarkers of pediatric mTBI. To address this important knowledge gap, this study introduced a multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based deep learning approach toward the classification of mTBI as compared with mild orthopedic injury (OI) by considering both structural MRI (sMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Firstly, convolutional features were extracted by employing a pre-trained DenseNet to capture the morphological features of both modalities. Next, by employing Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis (DCCA), distinct features obtained from the sMRI and DTI data were integrated into a multi-modal embedding. The obtained DCCA fused compact multimodal features were then fed to a random forest (RF) classifier that was used to classify mTBI versus mild OI. Additionally, to visualize the intra-individually heterogeneous brain regions that DenseNet most heavily relied upon for making classification, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was applied to the DenseNet outcomes for both modalities. According to the experimental outcomes on the clinical dataset, the introduced multimodal deep learning strategy improved the classification accuracy by 8.6% (from 75.8% to 84.4%) and 7.8% (from 76.6% to 84.4%) when compared to the unimodal morphological features, as generated from sMRI and DTI.
keywords: Mild Traumatic Brain Injury;Deep Learning;Transfer Learning;Multi-modal;Explainable AI

title: Integrating Cognitive Science and AI for Skin Disorder Detection
journal: 2026 Innovations in Machine, Engineering, and Digital Conference (IMED)
authors: A. Kulkarni and P. Pawar and B. Pansare and H. Raje and R. Patil
abstract: Dermatological diagnosis has faith in heavily on expert visual interpretation nevertheless remains vulnerable to variability arising from inconsistent imaging conditions, inadequate specialist availability, and subjective assessment. To incorporate these challenges, this paper introduces CogDermNet, a conceptual framework for real-time diagnostic support that incorporates cognitive science principles with artificial intelligence for detection of various types of skin disorders. The presented architecture incorporates cognitive visual awareness, memory-augmented reasoning, and multimodal contextual incorporation to mimic human perceptual and analytical activities. CogDermNet is aimed to process dermoscopic and clinical images acquired in various real-world sceneries and to produce interpretable predictions accompanied by human-associated justifications. Even though the system has not yet endured clinical or experimental estimation, this case study explains its potential applicability in primary care triage, remote dermatology, and telemedicine systems. By grounding AI components in cognitive procedures, CogDermNet seeks to enhance transparency, decrease diagnostic vagueness, and support trustworthy decision-making in forthcoming dermatology applications.
keywords: Cognitive artificial intelligence;memory augmented reasoning;explainable AI;visual attention mechanism

title: Explainable Deep Learning Approach for Binary Kidney Stone Detection in CT Imaging Using MobileNetV2
journal: 2025 IEEE 7th International Conference on Sustainable Technologies For Industry 5.0 (STI)
authors: A. A. Ahmad and M. A. Johab and D. K. Dutta and M. A. Wadud and N. Tasnim and N. Aman
abstract: Accurate detection of kidney stones in axial CT images is essential for timely diagnosis and management, yet manual interpretation remains time-consuming and prone to inter-reader variability. To address this challenge, a deep learning-based explainable framework is proposed for binary classification of stone vs. non-stone cases. The dataset includes 3,364 original CT images and $\mathbf{3 5, 4 5 7}$ augmented images, all clinically verified, ensuring both reliability and diversity for robust training. Three convolutional neural networks-AlexNet, DenseNet121 and MobileNetV2-were evaluated under a unified transfer-learning strategy with standard augmentation and early-stopping. To enhance transparency, Explainable AI (XAI) techniques such as class-activation/Grad-CAM heatmaps were employed, providing visual localization of decision-critical regions consistent with radiological findings. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed MobileNetV2-based model achieved the highest classification accuracy of 99.72%, outperforming AlexNet and DenseNet121 while maintaining computational efficiency. The integration of XAI confirmed that the model’s predictions align with clinically relevant stone features, thereby improving interpretability and clinical trust. These findings highlight the potential of lightweight CNNs combined with explainability to deliver fast, accurate and interpretable decision-support tools for kidney stone detection in routine CT imaging, with applications in workflow triage, quality assurance and future prospective validation.
keywords: Kidney stone;CT imaging;deep learning;MobileNetV2;Explainable AI;medical image classification

title: AI-Driven Diagnostics and Predictive Maintenance in NPI Service Engineering: A Comprehensive Survey of Methods, Applications, and Future Directions
journal: 2025 4th International Conference on Smart Cities, Automation & Intelligent Computing Systems (ICON-SONICS)
authors: M. Godbole and A. Jadhav
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly transforming how complex electromechanical products are diagnosed, serviced, and maintained. However, their integration within the New Product Introduction (NPI) phase remains fragmented across design, manufacturing, and service domains. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of AI-driven diagnostics and predictive maintenance frameworks specifically applied in NPI Service Engineering. The study systematically reviews recent literature and industrial implementations to identify core techniques such as data-driven fault detection, digital twins, and physics-informed models, along with their roles in improving fault triage accuracy, mean time to repair (MTTR), and first-time fix rates (FTF). A structured taxonomy is developed to classify methods based on learning paradigms, data sources, and system hierarchy levels. Comparative analysis reveals that hybrid AI models-combining physical modeling with deep learning-offer the highest potential for early anomaly detection and cross-domain integration. Finally, the paper highlights research gaps in dataset standardization, model interpretability, and real-time deployment within field environments, offering a roadmap for future AI-augmented NPI ecosystems.
keywords: New Product Introduction (NPI);Service Engineering;Predictive Maintenance;Diagnostics;Artificial Intelligence (AI);Machine Learning (ML);Digital Twin;Federated Learning;Explainable AI (XAI)

title: Glaucoma Screening on Retinal Fundus Images with Deep Learning
journal: 2026 IEEE 5th International Multidisciplinary Conference on Engineering Technology (IMCET)
authors: A. Duru
abstract: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss, and effective screening relies on accurate identification of glaucomatous optic neuropathy from routine ocular imaging. Fundus photography is widely used as a supportive modality in clinical practice because it provides a direct view of the optic nerve head and adjacent retinal structures. In this study, a public retinal fundus dataset was used to evaluate the extent to which deep learning models can support glaucoma screening, while quantifying the effect of different backbone choices and hyperparameter configurations on performance. Training and evaluation pipeline was implemented considering a fair comparison across models. Under a matched experimental protocol, four convolutional neural networks were fine-tuned, including ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-B0, and ConvNeXt-Tiny. The best-performing configuration achieved ROC-AUC = 0.971, accuracy = 0.940 on the subject-level test folds, with sensitivity = 0.957 and specificity = 0.923. Model interpretability was further examined using Grad-CAM, and the resulting maps generally highlighted clinically relevant regions around the optic disc, providing qualitative support for the decision process. Overall, these findings suggest that automated glaucoma screening from retinal fundus images can serve as a useful component of clinical decision support systems for triage and prioritization.
keywords: Glaucoma detection;medical image classification;retinal fundus;artificial intelligence;deep learning

title: BioBridge: Unified Bio-Embedding With Bridging Modality in Code-Switched EMR
authors: J. Jeon and S. Cho and D. Lee and C. Lee and J. Kim
abstract: Pediatric Emergency Department (PED) overcrowding presents a significant global challenge, prompting the need for efficient solutions. This paper introduces the BioBridge framework, a novel approach that applies Natural Language Processing (NLP) to Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) in written free-text form to enhance decision-making in PED. In non-English speaking countries, such as South Korea, EMR data is often written in a Code-Switching(CS) format that mixes the native language with English, with most code-switched English words having clinical significance. The BioBridge framework consists of two core modules: “bridging modality in context” and “unified bio-embedding.” The “bridging modality in context” module improves the contextual understanding of bilingual and code-switched EMRs. In the “unified bio-embedding” module, the knowledge of the model trained in the medical domain is injected into the encoder-based model to bridge the gap between the medical and general domains. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed BioBridge significantly performance traditional machine learning and pre-trained encoder-based models on several metrics, including F1 score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision-recall Curve (AUPRC), and Brier score.
